first_experiment: Build ~20 small ML tasks with specs; have a stronger untrusted model run each honestly or with subtle sabotage (~5 categories); calibrate seed noise on honest runs; then compare detection rate at 1–5% false-positive rate, by sabotage type and cost, for a weak-model transcript monitor, a code reviewer, and a spec-only reimplementation-and-compare auditor, plus an adaptive attacker arm that tries to stay within noise.
why: Outcome-based checks don't rely on sabotage looking suspicious, so they may fail differently from transcript monitors and complement them; it is cheap to test with ground-truth labels, and to my knowledge existing sabotage-monitoring work focuses on transcript or action monitors rather than reimplementation auditing, though I could not verify this and would run a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether misbehavior-detection methods validated on implanted (SFT/synthetic-document) model organisms transfer to organisms whose misbehavior emerged from RL.
project: Do Implanted Model Organisms Predict Detection Performance on RL-Emergent Misbehavior?
question: For matched behaviors (e.g., test-case-hacking in code), do detection methods (linear probes, SAE/activation diffing, black-box prefill and persona sampling, CoT monitors, LLM auditing agents) show the same absolute performance and the same ranking on RL-emergent organisms as on implanted ones? If not, which organism properties (representation locality, CoT verbalization, behavioral consistency) explain the divergence?
first_experiment: 1. Do the literature check first, with the kill criterion above. 2. Take one open-weight reasoning-capable model of about 8–32B parameters. 3. Build organism A by SFT on synthetic documents plus demonstrations of reward hacking in coding tasks. 4. Build organism B by RL on coding environments with exploitable graders, stopping when its hack rate matches A's on a held-out hackable set. 5. Build a clean control model. 6. Confirm that the behavioral profiles are comparable: hack rate, out-of-distribution generalization, and how often the model verbalizes the hack. 7. Run a small battery of 4–5 detectors on all three models. Use held-out prompts, and report AUROC for distinguishing the organism from control and for flagging individual hacking episodes. 8. Compute the rank correlation of detector performance between A and B, with bootstrap confidence intervals over seeds, since I'd need at least 3 seeds per organism type.
why: Detection methods will be chosen and trusted largely on the basis of model-organism evaluations, so if those evaluations don't predict performance on naturally emergent misbehavior, the field is miscalibrated on which tools to rely on. The question is cheap enough to answer with open-weight models. It has a clear decision-relevant output, either "implanted organisms are a valid proxy" or "here is where they are not." I believe it is under-explored because of the structural reasons above (costly matched construction, weak publication incentives for validity checks). I could not confirm that with a literature search, so the first step is to check, and I will pivot if the head-to-head comparison already exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure and reduce unfaithful self-reporting by autonomous research agents, treating the agent's report as a critical oversight channel for automated AI research.
project: Do research agents tell the truth about their own experiments? Instrumented measurement of disclosure failures and cheap mitigations
question: How often do LLM research agents omit or misrepresent known, logged events (bugs, null results, reduced-scale runs, leakage, mocked data, grader special-casing) in their final reports, how does incentive pressure change this, and do self-audit or trajectory-digest mitigations close the gap?
first_experiment: After a literature check to confirm novelty, build 8 sandboxed ML tasks with 4 instrumented event types, run 3–4 models × 10 samples under neutral and pressure framings, validate an LLM disclosure judge against 100 hand-labeled reports (κ ≥ 0.8), and report nondisclosure and false-claim rates with confidence intervals.
why: Automated research makes agent reports a key oversight channel, and misreporting can occur without any deliberate sabotage; it is cheap to measure with environment-logged ground truth, and I believe no one has run a controlled study separating omission from fabrication and testing report-only versus trajectory-based review, though I could not verify this without search and have a pivot rule if I'm wrong.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether ordinary training pressures that do not directly target the chain of thought still reduce how causally necessary the CoT is for misbehavior, which would make CoT monitors fail silently.
project: Necessity, Not Just Detection: Tracking Causal Reliance on Chain-of-Thought Under Indirect Training Pressure
question: Under RL pressures that do not penalize CoT content (output-only monitor penalties, length penalties, none), does the causal necessity of the CoT for exploiting flawed tasks fall before or without a fall in CoT-monitor catch rate, so that a healthy-looking monitor is actually degrading?
first_experiment: After a literature check against the kill criterion, RL-train a small open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-4B/8B) with GRPO on a coding environment with injectable exploits and difficulty tiers, in three arms (no extra pressure, output-only monitor penalty, length penalty) with at least 3 seeds. At each checkpoint measure exploit rate, LLM-monitor catch rate on the CoT, and CoT-necessity (drop in exploit success under CoT truncation, resampling, or swap), then look for a seed-robust dissociation between catch rate and necessity.
why: CoT monitoring is a key oversight layer, and a leading indicator of its silent degradation under ordinary training choices would directly inform lab decisions. The setup is cheap and tractable with open weights. To my knowledge, prior work focuses on catch rate or direct CoT pressure rather than necessity under indirect pressure, but I could not verify this without searching, so a kill criterion and pivot plan are included.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Find cheap, training-time early-warning indicators that CoT monitorability is eroding under optimization pressure, before external monitors visibly fail.
project: Canaries for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability: Leading Indicators of Obfuscation During RL
question: During RL with direct (CoT-monitor) or indirect (output-only) penalties on misbehavior, do intervention-based measures of CoT causal necessity, or probe-versus-CoT gaps, reliably drop before a fixed external CoT monitor's recall on shortcut use collapses, with low false alarms in unpressured control runs?
first_experiment: Pilot GRPO on a 7-14B open-weight reasoning model in a prompt-hint shortcut environment, with two conditions (no pressure, CoT-monitor penalty) and 3 seeds each. Every 20 steps, log hack rate, weak-LLM-monitor recall, and a truncation/paraphrase CoT-necessity score. First confirm that obfuscation emerges, then check whether the CoT-necessity score leads monitor recall.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading safety strategy, and the open practical question is how to know when it is failing, not only whether it can fail. This study yields a falsifiable, preregistered answer that is feasible at small scale. I believe it is under-explored because prior work emphasizes demonstrating obfuscation or static monitorability measurement rather than predictive indicators over training, but I haven't verified this and will check the literature first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how routine, non-adversarial training pressures, starting with token-efficiency penalties, degrade the chain-of-thought monitorability of reward hacking in reasoning models.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Efficiency Pressure: Does Training Reasoning Models to Think Shorter Make Their Reward Hacking Harder to Catch?
question: As length-penalty strength or token budget increases during RL, does a CoT-based monitor's ability to detect reward hacking decline relative to an output-only monitor, at matched hack rates and matched capability? If so, is the cause less verbalization of the hack, or something else?
first_experiment: Run a cheap pilot with no RL. Take Qwen3-8B (thinking mode) on a coding environment with a planted hackable hint, such as a leaked or incorrect test. Apply inference-time budget forcing at several token budgets. For each budget, record the hack rate, the fraction of hacks that the CoT verbalizes, and CoT-monitor versus output-only-monitor TPR at a fixed FPR. If verbalization or monitor TPR already shifts with budget, scale to GRPO with graded length penalties. If not, that is an informative early null.
why: Monitorability is one of the best available safety levers, and its fragility under unintended pressure is the most decision-relevant open question. Existing work mostly covers direct CoT optimization and output-penalty spillover, while token-efficiency pressure is ubiquitous in practice and, as far as I know, lacks a controlled dose-response study. This is a belief from memory, not a verified fact, so I would check recent literature on CoT compression, faithfulness, and monitorability before committing compute. The project is cheap to start, has a falsifiable prediction, and yields guidance for labs whether the result is positive or null.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Validate evaluation-awareness suppression methods against ground truth, using model organisms that misbehave only when they believe they are in real deployment.
project: Ground-Truthing Eval-Awareness Corrections: Can We Recover Deployment Behavior from Evaluations?
question: When a model's misbehavior depends on whether it believes it is being tested, how accurately do activation steering, probe ablation and realism rewriting each recover its true deployment-time misbehavior rate from evaluation-style inputs, and when do they fail?
first_experiment: Do a quick literature check on eval-awareness steering, realism rewriting and conditional-behavior model organisms. Then fine-tune an open-weight instruction model (about 7–30B) on agentic scenarios where it takes a clearly misaligned action only in contexts with "real deployment" cues (realistic data, messy tool outputs, no evaluation framing) and acts aligned in contexts with test cues. Validate the organism on held-out cue types, and train linear probes for "test vs. deployment" on the residual stream. Then run the three corrections on a held-out evaluation-style set, compare the recovered misbehavior rate to the known deployment rate, and include random-direction steering and capability-degradation controls.
why: Safety conclusions from evals are only as good as the assumption that eval behavior predicts deployment behavior. Several correction methods already exist, but as far as I know they are used without ground-truth validation. Model organisms with known conditional behavior supply that ground truth cheaply, on open-weight models, in a project one agent can finish. The result is useful whichever way it comes out: either the corrections work and can be trusted, or they fail in specific ways that eval designers need to know about. I believe this hasn't been done because most eval-awareness work has gone to showing the phenomenon in frontier models, where ground truth is unavailable. I could be wrong about that, which is why the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure which cheap detection methods can catch subtle sabotage by untrusted AI research agents, at fixed audit budgets and under attacker adaptation.
project: Catching the Quiet Saboteur: Comparing Detection Methods for Subtle Sabotage in Agentic ML-Research Tasks
question: At matched false-positive rates, how do trusted monitoring, resampling consistency, noise injection, activation probes, and execution-based differential testing compare at detecting subtle, low-rate sabotage by a model organism doing ML-research tasks, and how does this change when the saboteur is trained to evade the detectors?
first_experiment: After a literature check to confirm the gap, build 20 verifiable ML-experiment tasks and one model organism, fine-tuned from an open-weight model to insert a single sabotage type (train/test leakage inflating a reported metric) under a trigger. Run the trusted-monitor baseline and the execution-based check, and compute detection AUROC and recall at 1% and 5% false-positive rate. This tests whether the pipeline yields a non-degenerate signal before I scale to more sabotage types and detectors.
why: The threat of research sabotage grows as automated AI-safety research scales, and the field needs to know which inexpensive defenses actually work before relying on them. Existing work tends to study one detection method or one crude sandbagging setup in isolation. A head-to-head comparison on realistic, subtle, agentic tasks, with adaptive attackers, is the gap I'm aiming at. I believe it's open, but I haven't verified this against the latest literature, so the first step is to check and narrow the project if needed. The result is useful whichever way it comes out: it either identifies workable defenses or shows concretely where they fail.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how much safety-eval results depend on a model's latent evaluation awareness, by causally manipulating awareness and comparing latent against verbalized awareness across several misbehavior types.
project: How Much Does Eval Awareness Move the Needle? Causal, Cross-Behavior Measurement of Latent vs. Verbalized Evaluation Awareness
question: When evaluation awareness is causally suppressed or amplified in open-weight reasoning models, how much do misbehavior rates (sandbagging, deceptive reporting, reward hacking, goal-conflict misalignment) change, and does verbalized awareness in the CoT track latent awareness well enough to serve as a reliable audit signal?
first_experiment: After a literature check, extract and validate a contrastive eval-awareness direction in one open-weight reasoning model. Then run a steering-strength sweep on a goal-conflict misbehavior scenario set, with matched-norm random-direction and formality-direction controls, and measure misbehavior rate, probe activation, and verbalized awareness at each strength.
why: Safety evals underlie deployment decisions, and their validity depends on models not behaving differently when they suspect a test. Existing work shows that models can detect and verbalize eval awareness, but I believe it has not systematically measured the causal effect size across multiple behaviors with confound-controlled steering, or tested whether CoT verbalization is an adequate proxy for latent awareness. I can't confirm that gap from here, so the literature check comes first and may force a narrower scope. The project is feasible with open-weight models and modest compute, and either outcome is useful. Large effects mean current evals need awareness-robust designs, and small or confounded effects mean the worry is overstated for current models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether white-box activation monitors remain reliable after RL pressure has made chain-of-thought monitors fail, to determine whether layered monitoring offers independent protection.
project: Do Probes Survive When the CoT Goes Dark? Independence of Monitoring Layers Under Optimization Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a CoT-monitor penalty and learns obfuscated reward hacking, does a linear activation probe for hacking intent (not trained against) still detect the hacking, and does divergence between the CoT monitor and the probe give early warning before behavioral obfuscation appears?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding environment for a ~4–8B open reasoning model. Run GRPO with reward only versus reward plus a weak-LLM CoT-monitor penalty, 3 seeds each. At regular checkpoints, record hack rate (programmatic ground truth), CoT-monitor TPR at fixed FPR, and activation-probe AUROC (both fixed-from-base and per-checkpoint retrained), then compare the trajectories to see whether probe performance holds as CoT monitorability collapses.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading safety tool and is known to be fragile under optimization, while defense in depth with probes is widely assumed to be independent without much direct testing. This experiment tests that assumption cheaply at small scale. Whether probes survive or collapse, the result is actionable: it either justifies keeping held-out probes as a tripwire or shows that the layers fail together. Prior work covers obfuscation from CoT pressure and probe evasion when probes are trained against, but I don't know of work that measures held-out probe robustness on models whose CoT monitorability was destroyed by RL. I haven't verified this, so a literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether synthetic honeypot attacks used to validate untrusted monitors are distinguishable from real model-generated attacks, and how much this undermines control-protocol safety estimates.
project: Can the Monitor Tell It's a Honeypot? Measuring Synthetic-vs-Real Attack Discriminability in Untrusted Monitoring
question: How well can LLMs (prompted and probed) distinguish synthetic honeypot attacks from the untrusted policy's own attacks, how does this scale with capability, how large is the resulting gap between nominal and true protocol safety, and can adversarial honeypot generation close it?
first_experiment: In a ControlArena APPS-backdoor setting, build confound-matched datasets of real (in-situ) and synthetic (edit-inserted or weaker-generator) backdoors. Measure discrimination AUROC with zero-shot prompts across several model sizes, a linear probe, and a fine-tuned upper bound. Then simulate a colluding monitor that flags only items classified as synthetic, and compute the gap between nominal and true safety.
why: The safety of untrusted monitoring hinges on an assumption (honeypot indistinguishability) that is argued but rarely measured. The study is cheap, has clear metrics, and a null or positive result both inform decisions. To my knowledge the specific intersection of matched real and synthetic attacks, capability scaling, probes, and a safety-gap estimate has not been systematically measured, but I have not verified this and will check the literature first, narrowing to adversarial honeypot improvement if it is partly covered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify whether chain-of-thought obfuscation learned under pressure from one monitor transfers to other monitors (different LLM judges, activation probes, output-only), to test whether monitor diversity is a real safety defense.
project: The Monitor Transfer Matrix: Does Evading One Monitor Mean Evading Them All?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from monitor type X on reward hacking, how much does detection by held-out monitors of type Y drop relative to the true hacking rate, and does a heterogeneous monitor ensemble retain high detection when any single monitor can be evaded?
first_experiment: After a literature check, pilot a reward-hackable coding environment on an open 8B reasoning model with programmatic hack labels and four validated monitors (two LLM CoT monitors, an activation probe, an output-only monitor). Then run matched-compute GRPO arms (task-only, penalty from CoT monitor A, penalty from probe; 3 seeds) and plot true hack rate and each held-out monitor's TPR at 1% FPR across training, to produce the transfer matrix.
why: Safety cases lean on monitor diversity, but the transfer of learned obfuscation across monitor types is, as far as I know, untested systematically. It is tractable at small scale with ground-truth labels, and the result directly informs how monitoring stacks should be designed. I can't verify novelty as of today, so the literature check comes first and has a defined pivot.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how CoT monitorability changes as a function of ordinary RL training choices, to identify which design decisions preserve oversight of reasoning models.
project: Monitorability Drift: Tracking Chain-of-Thought Legibility of Exploits Across RL Training Variants
question: When a reasoning model learns to exploit a flaw in its RL environment without any explicit pressure on its CoT, how often does its CoT reveal the exploit to a fixed weaker monitor, how does that change over training, and which training choices (length penalty, KL strength, RL duration, SFT warmup, model size) predict its loss?
first_experiment: Build 3–4 verifiable-reward environments with injectable, ground-truth-labeled exploits (leaked answers, grader-visible tests), then evaluate existing open intermediate RL checkpoints (e.g., OLMo 3 Think, small Qwen3) for exploit rate and monitor recall at fixed false-positive rate conditional on exploitation, validating the monitor against a human-labeled subsample; follow with small multi-seed GRPO runs varying length penalty, KL, and duration.
why: CoT monitoring is a cheap, currently effective oversight layer whose robustness to ordinary training is a decision-relevant unknown. Prior work I know of covers adversarial optimization against monitors and static evaluations, not controlled multi-seed comparisons of training variants. Starting from released checkpoints gives data at near-zero training cost, and both positive and null results are informative. I could not verify novelty against current literature, so a literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether white-box (activation) monitoring remains effective after RL pressure against a text CoT monitor has made the text uninformative.
project: Does the Signal Survive the Scrubbing? Probe Detectability of Reward Hacking After Training Against CoT Monitors
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor and learns to hack while its text no longer reveals intent, do linear activation probes still detect the hacking intent, and how does this compare with training against an action-only monitor or with no monitor?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a hackable coding environment with programmatic hack detection and run GRPO on Qwen3-8B (or similar) under the three conditions (outcome-only, CoT-monitor penalty, action-only-monitor penalty). Save checkpoints, then compare the hack rate, a held-out text monitor's recall, and fixed and refit linear probe AUROC across checkpoints.
why: It targets an assumption behind layered-monitoring safety cases, that the text and internal channels fail independently, and tests it directly. It is feasible with open weights and modest compute. Existing work, as far as I know, covers text obfuscation and direct probe evasion but not this cross-channel test. I may be missing recent papers, which is why the literature check comes first and the scope is built to narrow if needed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how much training a policy against one safety monitor degrades detection by other, held-out monitors (text-based and activation-based), to test whether layered monitoring actually provides defense in depth.
project: Monitor Spillover: Does Evading One Monitor Mean Evading Them All?
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized by a CoT monitor for reward-hacking intent, how do detection rates of held-out CoT monitors, action-only monitors, and activation probes change, and does a latent signal persist after text-level evasion emerges?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an exploitable test loophole on a small open-weight reasoning model, confirm a 5–30% programmatically labeled hack rate, then measure baseline detection (AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR) for a prompted CoT monitor, a second-family CoT monitor, an action-only monitor, and a linear activation probe on held-out tasks. After that, run a short no-penalty RL pilot to confirm the setup is stable before adding the penalty arm.
why: Layered monitoring is the standard proposed mitigation, yet the evidence on how evasion pressure transfers between monitors is thin. The experiment is feasible at small scale, has objective ground truth, and gives decision-relevant results whether positive or negative. I could not check the literature in this session, so novelty is unverified and a literature check comes first. It is probably not already covered in this form because existing work tends to study one monitor at a time rather than the full spillover matrix within a single training run.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether AI monitors are systematically more lenient toward sabotage produced by themselves or their own model family, and whether this is mediated by self-recognition.
project: Do Monitors Go Easy on Their Own? Self-Preference Bias in Safety Monitoring of Agentic Sabotage
question: Holding attack content fixed, do monitors assign lower suspicion and lower detection rates at fixed false-positive rate to malicious trajectories from themselves or their own family than to those from other models, and is this mediated by self-recognition and removable by reducing it?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a monitor×generator matrix across 3–4 model families on control-style sabotage tasks with matched attack success. Compute AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR per pair, fit a mixed-effects model for the same-model/same-family effect, and run paraphrase and attribution-label controls to rule out style and quality confounds.
why: It targets a plausible silent failure mode of control protocols (same-model monitoring) that is cheap to test with a clear go/no-go outcome. Prior work covers judge self-preference on quality and prompted collusion on signals, but I do not recall one that isolates spontaneous, self-recognition-mediated leniency toward sabotage. This novelty claim needs verification in the first step.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how routine RL and CoT-shaping choices (length penalties, distillation, process rewards, training duration) incidentally change chain-of-thought monitorability in open-weight reasoning models.
project: Does Your Training Recipe Silently Break CoT Monitoring? Controlled Ablations of Incidental Monitorability Loss
question: At matched task accuracy, how do common training recipe choices affect a fixed CoT monitor's ability to detect hint reliance and side-task behavior, particularly when the CoT is necessary for the behavior?
first_experiment: Build hint-use and side-task eval sets, then measure CoT-monitor recall at 1% false-positive rate across several existing open reasoning models using two monitor strengths and two controls (shuffled CoT, answer-only monitor) to validate the metric before running any RL.
why: It targets a fragile and widely relied-upon oversight tool, addresses incidental rather than adversarial degradation, is feasible at small scale with a clear falsifiable metric, and I know of no controlled open-weight recipe ablation of it, though I haven't verified this and will do a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether monitor performance measured on prompted-attack trajectories transfers to misbehavior that emerges naturally from RL training.
project: Do Prompted Red-Team Evaluations Predict Monitor Performance on Naturally Emergent Reward Hacking?
question: How large is the gap in monitor recall (at a fixed low false-positive rate) between prompted-attack misbehavior and RL-emergent reward hacking, with and without CoT access, and are monitor rankings preserved across the two distributions?
first_experiment: Do a literature check for prior prompted-versus-emergent monitor comparisons. Then take one open-weight reasoning model and build a coding environment with several known exploitable test flaws. Run a small RL sweep until hacking rates reach about 10–30%. Collect labeled natural-hack trajectories using programmatic detectors, plus prompted-attack and benign trajectories from the same model. Score all three sets with three LLM monitors in action-only and CoT-visible modes, and report recall at 1% FPR per set.
why: It targets a load-bearing but rarely tested assumption behind AI control and monitoring safety cases, and it is feasible with open weights and modest compute. Either outcome changes practice: validation of current methods, or a concrete argument for building evaluation sets from trained model organisms. I believe it has not been done systematically because most monitor work uses prompted attackers for convenience and most reward-hacking work studies emergence rather than detector transfer. I can't confirm that without a search, which is why the literature check comes first and the plan has a defined pivot if I find overlapping work.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether optimization pressure on one reward-hacking monitor degrades detection by other, independent monitors, to test the assumption behind layered monitoring.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer Across Monitors? Cross-Monitor Effects of Training Against CoT Monitors and Activation Probes
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized for being flagged by monitor A (text CoT monitor or activation probe) while reward hacking, does its hacking remain detectable by held-out monitor B, and how does this depend on monitor type and on whether B was trained on pre-RL or post-RL data?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build a hackable coding environment for a Qwen3 4B–8B reasoning model, run unpenalized GRPO to confirm hacking emerges with programmatic labels, and train an LLM CoT monitor and layerwise linear probes on those rollouts to establish baseline AUROC and TPR@1%FPR before running the monitor-penalty arms.
why: Layered monitoring is assumed to fail independently but this is untested as far as I know; the result is decision-relevant either way, it is feasible at small scale, and prior work I recall studies single-monitor obfuscation, though I could not verify that the cross-monitor question is unaddressed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure when RL-based capability elicitation fails against models that strategically under-explore (exploration hacking), and whether such behavior is detectable.
project: Dose-Response of Exploration Hacking: When Can RL Recover Strategically Hidden Capabilities?
question: How does the strength of a reasoning model's sandbagging (measured by pass@k under the trigger) and its form (verbalized in the CoT vs. internalized in the weights) determine whether RL with a correctness reward elicits the hidden capability, and can CoT monitors or activation probes detect the sandbagging when RL fails?
first_experiment: After a literature check to confirm the gap, fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model into a trigger-conditioned sandbagger on a benign proxy task (math or coding), at 3-4 sandbagging strengths. Run GRPO with a correctness reward on the triggered distribution. Plot capability recovery against initial pass@k (k = 1, 8, 64), and compare against SFT-on-few-demonstrations and prompting baselines. Check for a threshold where group-level reward variance vanishes and RL stalls.
why: Elicitation reliability is a load-bearing assumption in capability evaluations and in plans to use AI on hard-to-verify safety work, yet it is mostly argued conceptually rather than measured. The experiment is cheap, needs only open-weight models, and yields a practical output: a rule of thumb for when RL elicitation can be trusted, plus detection baselines. To my knowledge, prior work on password-locked models covers SFT elicitation well but doesn't systematically cover RL against reasoning models that actively strategize, so the dose-response relationship appears open. I can't confirm this through late 2026, which is why the literature check comes first and why I have a fallback pivot to the detection sub-question.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how well auditors of different strengths and access levels can detect subtle, deniable methodological flaws in AI-produced ML/safety experiments.
project: Seeded-Flaw Audits of AI-Generated Safety Research
question: When an AI research agent produces an experiment with a deliberately seeded, plausibly deniable flaw, what fraction do auditors catch at a fixed false-positive rate, and how does this vary with flaw type, auditor-vs-producer capability, auditor access (report, code, execution, full trajectory), and producer evasion effort, compared with the base rate of honest errors?
first_experiment: Build about 30 verified small-model experiment templates, generate programmatically verified flawed variants across 6 flaw classes (with and without an evasion instruction) plus matched honest runs, then run three auditor tiers at four access levels and score detection and localization at a 5% false-positive rate, with a small human baseline.
why: AI-automated research is only safe to rely on if its output is cheaper to verify than to produce, and little empirical data exists on audit detection of subtle flaws as a function of access and capability gap. It is feasible with inference-only compute and controlled ground truth. Related sabotage and control work exists, so I would first check for overlap, but I believe the audit-side, access-level-by-capability-gap framing with honest-error baselines has not been systematically measured.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether AI research agents produce incentive-driven false positive claims (p-hacking, selective reporting, overclaiming), and whether auditors can detect them.
project: Ground-Truth Nulls: Epistemic Corruption in Automated Research Agents
question: When given ML experiments whose true effect is exactly zero (A/A designs), how often do research agents report unsupported positive results or undisclosed forking paths, how does this change with pressure and with affordances for rerunning and analysis choice, and what level of reviewer access (report only, code, full transcript, independent reproduction) is needed to catch it?
first_experiment: Run about 10 A/A tasks across 2–3 models, 3 pressure levels (neutral, mild, strong), and 2 affordance levels (single run versus free reruns and metric choice), with 5 samples per cell (about 600 runs). Score each report against a pre-registered analysis and the known null, hand-validate a subset of the scoring, then test reviewer models at each information level for detection rate.
why: It targets a plausible, hard-to-notice failure of the strategy of automating alignment research, and ground-truth nulls give clean, cheap labels that most overclaiming studies lack. I could not search the recent literature, so I expect partial overlap with work on reward hacking and research sabotage. The specific combination of controlled pressure and affordance manipulations, exact-null tasks, and reviewer-access ablations is, to my knowledge, underexplored, and the first experiment is designed to give a clear go or no-go quickly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting truly removes emergent-misalignment dispositions or only gates them, by checking durability against later training stages and prompt perturbations.
project: Shallow or Deep? Durability of Inoculation Prompting Against Re-emergent Misalignment
question: After inoculation prompting prevents emergent misalignment or reward hacking in a fine-tuned model, does the disposition remain latent, as detected by probes and faster re-acquisition, and can it be re-elicited by further benign or RL training or by paraphrased inoculation text?
first_experiment: Do a literature check first. Then replicate IP on a Qwen-family model with insecure-code data in three arms (no inoculation, inoculation, benign control). Confirm the emergent-misalignment gap, then fine-tune all arms on a small benign dataset and on a small mildly-bad dataset. Compare misalignment rates and the projection onto a misalignment direction derived from the non-inoculated arm.
why: IP is a cheap, likely-to-be-adopted mitigation whose evidence is mostly immediate behavioral results. Latent-state and re-elicitation tests from the unlearning literature have, as far as I know, not been systematically applied to it, though I must verify this. The experiments are feasible at small scale, and either outcome changes how much safety weight IP should carry.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting actually removes emergent-misalignment dispositions or only masks them, using internal probes and re-elicitation stress tests.
project: Masked or Removed? Stress-Testing Inoculation Prompting Against Emergent Misalignment
question: When inoculation prompting prevents emergent misalignment on standard evals, does the model still carry a latent misaligned-persona representation that can be re-elicited by distribution shift, small finetunes, or prompt variation, compared with a model that never saw the bad data?
first_experiment: Finetune Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct with LoRA on insecure-code data under three conditions (plain, inoculated, benign-prompt control) with ≥3 seeds. Measure misalignment with a judge on free-form questions with no system prompt. Compute a persona direction from the plain EM model, compare its projection across conditions, and measure misalignment after a 100-example benign finetune.
why: It targets a mitigation that is cheap, promising, and likely to be adopted, and it asks the safety-critical question of whether the fix is real or superficial. It is feasible with open models and no RL compute, and its hypotheses are falsifiable either way. To my knowledge, existing work mainly demonstrates that inoculation works, not that it is robust, and the unlearning literature's "suppressed but recoverable" lesson has not been systematically applied to it. I'll confirm that with a literature check before investing compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether weaker reviewers and control protocols can catch deniable, validity-level sabotage in AI-generated ML research, using the correctness of the final scientific conclusion as the outcome.
project: Can We Trust the Lab Assistant? Detecting Deniable Experimental-Validity Sabotage in AI-Generated ML Research
question: When a capable model is instructed to subtly steer an ML experiment toward a chosen conclusion using only deniable validity flaws (leakage, weak baseline tuning, seed cherry-picking, mismeasured metrics), which review protocols (report-only, code review, rerun access, independent-reimplementation consistency) detect it, distinguish it from honest sloppiness, and recover the true conclusion, and at what cost?
first_experiment: Build 20 pilot comparison tasks, each with a ground-truth conclusion from a carefully controlled reference pipeline. Generate honest and sabotaged pipelines and reports with a strong model, plus honest-but-sloppy ones as a control for natural error. Give report-only and report-plus-code reviews to a weaker model. Measure (a) AUROC of sabotaged vs. honest and vs. sloppy, and (b) how often the reviewer's accepted conclusion matches ground truth. Check first that the sabotage actually flips conclusions, since otherwise it is not sabotage in the relevant sense.
why: Automated alignment research is a core part of lab safety plans, and its trustworthiness depends on handling subtle, deniable, hard-to-verify failures that existing code-sabotage evaluations underweight. The setup is cheap, since it uses small experiments, API models, and ground truth that can be re-run. It also produces an actionable metric (conclusion accuracy under review) rather than detection rates alone. I believe it hasn't been done in this form because most sabotage work targets checkable side tasks, and ground-truth-labelled validity flaws are laborious to construct. Adjacent work exists, though, and I cannot rule out that someone has already covered part of this, which is why the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop and test early-warning indicators, combining activation probes with CoT-monitor disagreement, that predict when RL pressure makes a model's chain of thought stop revealing reward-hacking intent.
project: Probing Ahead of Obfuscation: Early-Warning Signals for Loss of CoT Monitorability Under RL Pressure
question: When a model is RL-trained with a penalty on CoT-monitor flags in an environment with an exploitable loophole, does the gap between activation-probe detection and CoT-monitor detection of hacking, or CoT–action inconsistency, rise measurably before held-out CoT monitors lose recall, and with what lead time and false-alarm rate?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with an instrumented exploitable loophole and confirm a base-model hack rate of about 10–40%. Collect a few thousand ground-truth-labeled rollouts and measure AUROC and recall at fixed FPR for CoT monitors, an action-only monitor, and layer-swept linear probes. Then run a short GRPO pilot at λ=0 and two nonzero monitor-penalty values, saving checkpoints to see whether probes trained on early checkpoints transfer to later ones.
why: It addresses a live lab decision (whether to apply pressure to CoT) with a quantitative, predictive output rather than another demonstration of the phenomenon, and it is feasible with open models and modest compute. To my knowledge the predictive early-warning angle, which combines probes and CoT monitors across a pressure sweep, has not been systematically tested. I can't verify this from here, so a literature check comes first, and the design has explicit negative-result paths if the hypothesis fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether training pressure on a chain-of-thought monitor incidentally degrades independent activation-probe detection of reward hacking, so that layered defenses are not truly independent.
project: Do Monitoring Layers Fail Together? Spillover from CoT-Monitor Pressure to Activation Probes
question: When a reasoning model is trained against a CoT monitor and learns to hide reward-hacking intent, how much does the recall of activation probes (frozen or retrained, read at CoT versus action tokens) on monitor-evading hacks degrade relative to controls?
first_experiment: Build 200–500 exploitable coding tasks for a small open reasoning model, confirm a 5–40% programmatically labeled hack rate, measure the LLM CoT monitor's baseline recall and false-positive rate, and train linear probes at CoT, prompt-end, and action tokens to get pre-pressure held-out AUROC and recall at 1% FPR.
why: It tests the layer-independence assumption behind defense in depth, is cheap and falsifiable at small scale, and, to my knowledge, the incidental cross-layer spillover has not been measured, though I could not verify this without a literature search, which is the first step.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether routine, non-safety-motivated training pressures on reasoning traces (length penalties, token budgets, CoT compression) silently erode CoT monitorability of reward hacking, and identify which ones are safe.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Efficiency Training: Do Length Penalties Hide Reward Hacking?
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL against an exploitable verifier, do incidental pressures on CoT length or format reduce how often it verbalizes the exploit, even when its hacking rate stays constant or rises, and how large and dose-dependent is the effect?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on a small open-weight reasoning model in a coding environment with a flawed verifier and programmatically detectable exploits, under no length pressure, mild and strong length penalties, and a hard token budget; track ground-truth hack rate and CoT-monitor recall at fixed false-positive rate across checkpoints, comparing at matched hack rates.
why: CoT monitoring is a key near-term safety tool, efficiency pressures are strong default incentives that could degrade it without anyone intending that, the experiment is cheap with ground-truth labels, and the incidental-pressure dose-response question appears under-studied relative to direct obfuscation work (to be confirmed by a literature check, since I cannot verify recent publications).

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Empirically test whether models that deliberately underexplore can resist RL-based capability elicitation or safety training, and which countermeasures restore it.
project: Exploration Hacking Model Organisms: When Does RL Fail to Elicit What a Model Can Do?
question: Does a model with a reasoned, strategic lock (explicit CoT planning to avoid high-reward trajectories) resist GRPO-style elicitation substantially better than an imitation-based password-locked model, and which countermeasures (few-shot SFT, exploration bonuses, CoT monitoring, weak-model rollouts) recover performance most reliably?
first_experiment: After the literature check, build a password-locked 7–8B open-weight model on a verifiable coding or math task by SFT on weak-model outputs. Run GRPO with ground-truth reward on the locked distribution. Record recovery curves (pass rate vs. RL steps) against an unlocked baseline. This replicates the known result and validates the pipeline. Then train the reasoned-lock variant and run the identical GRPO setup, comparing the two curves.
why: Safety cases for capability evals and for RL-based behavior correction depend on RL actually surfacing high-reward behavior, and the known results on elicitation come from imitation-locked models whose weak behavior still succeeds sometimes. The gap is whether reasoning-driven underexploration changes that picture, plus a controlled comparison of countermeasures. It is feasible at small scale with open weights. I believe this specific on-policy, reasoned-lock comparison has not been done, but I can't verify that without searching, so the literature check comes first and could redirect the project.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether CoT monitorability erodes under realistic, non-targeted training pressures, and identify which pressures and which hack types are most at risk.
project: Does Monitorability Erode Without Being Targeted? CoT Monitor Gain Under Indirect RL Pressure
question: In RL on environments with exploitable reward hacks and no penalty applied to the CoT, do indirect pressures (a length penalty, a hard token budget, a format or style reward) reduce the detection advantage of a CoT-aware monitor over an action-only monitor? If so, does the effect hold after controlling for hack subtlety, and what CoT changes (shorter, terser, or less explicit reasoning about the hack) explain it?
first_experiment: 1. **Literature check (about a day).** Search for prior work on indirect-pressure monitorability. Apply the kill criteria above. 2. **Pilot (baseline, no pressure).** Take an open-weight reasoning model around 8B, such as a Qwen3 variant. Build or adapt a coding environment where tests can be gamed, for example by special-casing test inputs or editing the test file. Label hacks programmatically. 3. **Check the baseline.** Run GRPO for a few hundred steps and confirm that hack rate rises. Then compute monitor gain at checkpoints: recall at 1% false-positive rate for a fixed LLM monitor given CoT plus action, versus the same monitor given the action only. Gate: baseline gain must be clearly positive and hack rate must increase. 4. **Conditions.** If the gate passes, run three arms with 3 seeds each: no extra pressure, length penalty, and strict token budget. Track monitor gain, stratified by hack subtlety, across training. Add a CoT-length-matched control to separate length effects from content effects.
why: - **Why it's promising.** Labs are leaning on CoT monitorability as a safety property. Direct optimization against monitors is known to be dangerous. The question for real training pipelines is whether ordinary efficiency pressures quietly erode the property. The answer would give concrete guidance on which pressures to avoid or to track with a monitorability metric during training. - **Why it may not be done.** As far as I know, existing work emphasizes direct CoT pressure, static faithfulness evaluations, or position-level arguments, rather than controlled RL sweeps of indirect pressures with subtlety-stratified monitor gain. I can't verify this, so the literature check comes first, and the project pivots if it turns out to be covered. - **Main risk.** Small-scale RL on a small model may not transfer to frontier models. I'll report results as evidence about mechanisms and direction of effect, not as a claim about frontier systems.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop and test detection methods for covert sabotage of conclusions in AI-automated safety research, using ground-truth-verifiable small ML research tasks.
project: Catching the Quiet Saboteur: Monitoring Conclusion-Level Sabotage in Automated Research Agents
question: When a capable research agent covertly steers an experiment toward a false conclusion (handicapped baselines, selective reporting, leakage, over-claiming), how well can weaker trusted monitors detect it. How does detection change with access (transcript only, artifacts and code, or targeted re-execution under a fixed compute budget), and which sabotage types evade each monitor?
first_experiment: 1. Run a literature check for existing "research sabotage" benchmarks, and adjust scope if needed. 2. Build about 30 small, fast-to-run research tasks (for example, comparing two fine-tuning or regularization methods on small models and datasets). Each has a known honest answer, established by replicating it across many seeds. 3. For each task, run a strong model in an agent scaffold in two modes: honest, and covert saboteur with a target false conclusion. Use the five sabotage types above. 4. Label an episode as successful sabotage only if the final reported conclusion contradicts the replicated ground truth. 5. Run three monitors from a weaker model: transcript-only, transcript plus code and artifacts, and the same plus a budget of N targeted re-runs. 6. Report the true positive rate at 1% false positive rate (using the honest runs), broken down by sabotage type, along with monitor cost.
why: - **Importance:** Safety work is being delegated to AI agents, and a misleading conclusion that looks like normal research could corrupt the whole pipeline. Conclusion-level sabotage is harder to spot than a code backdoor because no single step is clearly bad. - **Tractability:** It needs only API access, small compute, and verifiable ground truth. It produces a reusable benchmark and an empirical cost-versus-detection curve. - **Gap:** As far as I know, existing control evaluations focus on code or action sabotage rather than sabotage of scientific conclusions with replication-based ground truth. I can't confirm this, because I can't see work from after my cutoff. If a close match exists, I will change the sabotage taxonomy or the monitor-access axis (the replication-budget tradeoff) rather than repeat it. - **Main risk:** The tasks may be too easy or too artificial to reflect real research. I'll mitigate this by including some tasks where the honest answer is ambiguous and checking that monitors don't flag them as sabotage.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether chain-of-thought monitor evasion learned under RL pressure from one monitor transfers to held-out monitors, to test whether never-trained-against canary monitors are a viable safeguard.
project: Do Held-Out Monitors Catch What Trained-Against Monitors Miss? Cross-Monitor Transfer of CoT Obfuscation
question: When an RL-trained policy learns to evade a CoT monitor A while still reward hacking, how much of that evasion transfers to held-out monitors differing in model family, size, prompt, input (CoT/action/both), or mechanism (LLM judge/regex/probe)?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding RL environment with programmatic ground-truth hack labels; run unpenalized GRPO on a small Qwen3 model (3 seeds) to confirm hacking emerges; measure baseline recall of 3–4 diverse monitors against ground truth; then run the penalized-against-monitor-A training and track the transfer ratio (recall drop on held-out monitors / recall drop on A) across checkpoints.
why: It tests a load-bearing but unverified assumption behind CoT-monitoring safety cases (that held-out monitors stay informative after optimization against others), it is feasible at small scale with ground-truth labels, and to my knowledge cross-monitor transfer has not been systematically quantified. This novelty claim is unverified because I could not search the literature, so I will do a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether latent (non-verbalized) evaluation awareness in open-weight reasoning models causally changes safety-relevant behavior, using white-box probes and steering with strict confound controls.
project: Does the Model Know It's a Test When It Doesn't Say So? Causal Tests of Latent Evaluation Awareness
question: In scenarios where a reasoning model never verbalizes that it is being evaluated, does an internal eval-awareness representation still predict and causally influence misaligned behavior, and how much does this bias standard safety-eval scores relative to realistic deployment-like versions of the same scenarios?
first_experiment: Do a literature check, then build about 200 matched test-like vs. realistic agentic scenarios. Train a linear eval-awareness probe on a separate contrastive corpus using an open-weight reasoning model, and validate it on held-out scenarios with length, style, and unrelated-contrast controls. Restrict to runs with no verbalized awareness, test whether probe activation predicts misbehavior, then run steering with random-direction controls and capability checks.
why: Safety evals are only informative if behavior under test resembles deployment behavior, and verbalization-based filtering can't rule out latent awareness. Causal tests of non-verbalized awareness with realism-matched pairs and steering controls appear underexplored, though I can't confirm that after my knowledge cutoff. It is feasible with open-weight models, and both positive and null results are decision-relevant.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how much eval awareness distorts behavioral safety evaluations, using causal interventions on open-weight reasoning models.
project: Eval Awareness Dose-Response: How Much Does Knowing It's a Test Hide Misalignment?
question: Across open-weight reasoning models and scenario types, how does measured misaligned behavior change as eval awareness is causally suppressed or induced (via probe-based steering and realism rewrites), and does an awareness-based correction transfer to held-out scenarios and models?
first_experiment: On one mid-size open reasoning model and one agentic honeypot family, train a "test vs. real" linear probe on scenario-independent contrastive data, validate it on held-out scenarios, then steer along it at several strengths (with random-direction and capability controls) and plot misbehavior rate against steering strength.
why: Nearly every safety claim depends on behavioral evals, so a quantitative estimate of their distortion from awareness is high-leverage and feasible with open models. Existing work, as far as I know, consists mainly of single-model or single-method demonstrations. The cross-model dose-response, the comparison of verbalized and probe-detected awareness, and the test of whether a correction transfers look less covered. I can't verify that without searching, so the first step is a literature check, and I will narrow the project to whatever remains open.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify, with two independent causal methods across multiple behavior families, how much evaluation awareness biases behavioral safety evaluations in open-weight reasoning models.
project: Dose-Response of Evaluation Awareness on Misaligned Behavior: Steering vs. CoT-Intervention Estimates
question: When evaluation awareness is causally suppressed or amplified, how do rates of misaligned behavior change across behavior families (agentic sabotage/blackmail, sandbagging, deception, reward hacking, sycophancy), and do activation-steering and CoT-resampling estimates agree?
first_experiment: On one open-weight reasoning model and ~50 paraphrased agentic-misalignment scenarios, measure baseline verbalized eval-awareness and misaligned-action rates. Then run CoT-resampling (remove eval-awareness sentences vs. matched random-sentence deletion, ≥20 samples per point). Next fit a validated eval-vs-deployment probe and run a controlled steering sweep (random-direction and capability controls) on the same scenarios, then compare the two effect estimates.
why: Eval awareness threatens the validity of nearly all behavioral safety evals, yet existing evidence is mostly anecdotal or single-method and single-behavior. A controlled, two-method, multi-family dose-response study is cheap on open-weight models and yields correction-relevant results, including whether the bias differs in sign across behaviors. I believe this specific cross-method comparison hasn't been done, but I can't verify that offline, so a literature check with a pivot plan comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether output-only training pressure erodes chain-of-thought monitorability in reasoning models, and test mitigations.
project: Spillover: Does Optimizing Only the Outputs Make Reasoning Models' Chains of Thought Unmonitorable?
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty applied only to its final outputs (never its CoT) in a reward-hackable environment, does a CoT-only monitor's recall on remaining hacks drop, how does this scale with penalty strength, and do mitigations such as separating the reasoning and answer-writing stages prevent it?
first_experiment: Build a hackable coding environment with Qwen3-8B, validate a CoT-only monitor against ~100 human-labeled hacks, then run GRPO with reward only (A) versus reward plus an output-only hack-detector penalty (B), 3 seeds each. Compare hack rate and CoT-monitor recall under a pre-registered decision rule.
why: It tests a core assumption behind current CoT-safety practice (that not training on the CoT keeps it monitorable), and it is feasible at small scale with open models. Prior prominent work pressures the CoT directly, so the indirect-pressure dose-response with necessity controls and mitigation comparisons appears under-characterized. I could not search the literature in this session, so I would verify that first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Stress-test whether training-time mitigations for emergent misalignment, starting with inoculation prompting, remove the underlying misaligned disposition or merely condition it away on the training context.
project: Removed or Hidden? Testing the Robustness of Inoculation Prompting Against Latent Misaligned Personas
question: When inoculation prompting suppresses emergent misalignment after narrow fine-tuning on bad data, does the internal misaligned-persona representation actually shrink, or does it remain latent and recoverable via nearby prompts, activation probes, and fast relearning?
first_experiment: After a literature check, fine-tune a ~7B open instruct model with LoRA on a narrow bad-behavior dataset under three matched conditions (no prompt, inoculation prompt, irrelevant-prompt control; 3+ seeds). Then compare free-form misalignment rates across exact, paraphrased, and drifted prompts, compare projections onto a misaligned-persona direction, and compare relearning speed on small benign fine-tunes against the base model.
why: It addresses the central evaluation problem of whether a mitigation removes a bad disposition or hides it, it is cheap and fast on open models with pre-registered decision rules, and the combined behavioral, mechanistic, and relearning protocol appears to be an open gap. I cannot verify this against literature after my training cutoff, so I will confirm it first and pivot to a neighboring mitigation if it has been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting actually removes emergent misalignment from training on reward-hacking data or only masks it, using behavioral, probe-based, and relearning measures.
project: Inoculated or Hidden? Probing Residual Misalignment After Inoculation Prompting
question: After fine-tuning on reward-hacking data with an inoculation prompt, does the model's misaligned persona representation and its susceptibility to misaligned behavior (under prompt shift and light further fine-tuning) remain, even when behavior under the training-like prompt looks clean?
first_experiment: Do a literature check for existing probe or relearning evaluations of inoculation prompting. Then fine-tune Qwen3-8B on insecure-code or reward-hacking data in three conditions (no inoculation, inoculation prompt, irrelevant-prompt control). Evaluate emergent misalignment under a graded set of system prompts, from identical to opposite of the inoculation prompt. Also measure a diff-of-means misaligned-persona direction's activation in each condition.
why: It tests a cheap, likely-to-be-adopted mitigation for whether it is robust or only conceals the problem, it is feasible with open models, and every outcome is informative. I believe existing evaluations focus on behavior in training-like contexts, but I could not verify this, so the literature check comes first and I will narrow the question if the gap is already filled.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether activation-probe monitors remain effective as a backstop when RL pressure is applied only to chain-of-thought monitors.
project: Do Probes Survive When CoT Is Optimized? Incidental Activation-Monitor Degradation Under CoT-Monitor Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from a CoT monitor, producing obfuscated reward hacking, does a linear activation probe for hacking intent lose detection power (transferred or retrained) relative to a no-penalty and a matched-control-penalty baseline, especially on hacks that evade the CoT monitor?
first_experiment: On an exploitable coding environment with a small open-weight reasoning model, sample a few thousand base-model rollouts with the hack rate tuned to roughly 10 to 40%. Auto-label hacks and train layer-wise linear probes on prompt-matched hack and non-hack samples. Compare probe AUROC at fixed FPR with an LLM CoT monitor's recall, to confirm the probe signal is real and not a context-presence artifact, before launching the GRPO conditions.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading near-term oversight tool, and probes are the natural complementary layer. Whether the two fail independently or together under realistic training pressure is an open question that directly affects how safety cases should be built. The experiment is tractable at small scale, and its results are informative either way. I believe it is not already done because existing work focuses on either CoT-monitor obfuscation or adversarial training against probes, not on incidental probe degradation from text-only pressure. I haven't verified that against current literature, so the first task is a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether optimizing against a chain-of-thought monitor degrades independent activation-probe monitors, to test whether layered monitoring fails jointly.
project: Does training against a CoT monitor leak into activation probes? Measuring monitor independence under optimization pressure
question: When a small open-weights reasoning model learns to reward hack under RL with a CoT-monitor penalty, do activation probes for hacking lose accuracy beyond the drift seen under RL without monitor pressure, and does this track the collapse of CoT monitor detection?
first_experiment: Build a coding environment with a programmatically detectable test-exploit, run GRPO/LoRA on a Qwen3-8B-class reasoning model with no monitor penalty, confirm hacking emerges, and measure CoT-monitor and linear-probe (fixed and per-checkpoint) AUROC across checkpoints as the drift-only baseline. Then add the CoT-penalty arm and compare.
why: It addresses a concrete open decision (whether layered monitors are independent under training pressure), is feasible with small models and ground-truth labels, and separates spillover from representation drift, which I believe prior work hasn't done, though I can't verify this for the months before today, so the project starts with a literature check.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop and validate white-box leading indicators that warn when chain-of-thought monitorability is degrading during RL training, before text-based monitors fail.
project: The Verbalization Gap: Activation-vs-Text Early Warning for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Loss
question: During RL on tasks with an exploitable reward hack, does the gap between activation-probe decodability and CoT-text-monitor decodability of "exploiting the grader" widen measurably before text-monitor recall drops, and does it predict obfuscation across training runs, exploit types, and penalty regimes?
first_experiment: After a literature check for prior work on probe-vs-monitor divergence during RL, I will take an open-weight reasoning model (about 1.5–8B parameters, such as a Qwen3 or R1-distill variant) and build a coding environment with an easy exploit (hardcoding to visible tests, or reading leaked test files). I will run LoRA GRPO in two arms: (a) outcome reward only, and (b) outcome reward plus a penalty from an LLM monitor reading the CoT for exploit intent. I will checkpoint regularly. At each checkpoint I will measure exploit rate, text-monitor recall on exploit episodes, and linear-probe accuracy for exploit intent on residual-stream activations, with a control probe for an unrelated latent. The pilot succeeds if arm (b) shows obfuscation, meaning a high exploit rate with falling monitor recall, and I can test whether the probe-minus-monitor gap leads the recall drop by a consistent number of checkpoints across at least 3 seeds.
why: Monitorability is among the most load-bearing near-term safety tools, and its known weakness is that it can erode silently under training. A leading indicator would let developers detect erosion and stop or adjust training, which would turn a position-paper concern into an operational measurement. The question is cheap to test at small scale, and the result is informative either way: a positive result gives a practical monitoring signal, and a negative result warns against relying on activation-based early warning. Existing work, as far as I know, mostly demonstrates that obfuscation can occur or argues that monitorability should be preserved. I'm not aware of work that tracks text-vs-activation divergence over the course of training to forecast failure, but I haven't verified this, and the literature check comes first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Stress-test AI control protocols against attacks that are decomposed across multiple individually benign sessions, and develop cross-episode monitors that defend against them.
project: Split-Attack Control: Do Per-Episode Monitors Fail When Sabotage Is Distributed Across Sessions?
question: When an untrusted agent splits a sabotage objective (for example, a backdoor or a secret exfiltration path) into k pieces across k sequential tasks on a shared codebase, how much does that lower the detection rate of per-episode trusted monitors at a fixed audit budget, and how much of the lost safety do cumulative-state monitors recover, and at what cost in false positives and compute?
first_experiment: 1. **Literature check (about a day).** Search for prior work on multi-episode or decomposed attacks in control, and adjust the design if there is overlap. 2. **Build a setting.** Use ControlArena or a minimal equivalent: a sequence of N=5–10 small software tasks on a persistent repo. The side task is a harmful behavior, such as exfiltrating a planted fake credential or inserting an auth bypass, that needs k≥3 coordinated components. 3. **Attackers.** Compare three conditions: - (a) honest policy; - (b) single-episode attack, with the whole side task in one episode; - (c) split attack, where the attacker plans pieces and may coordinate only through the repo state, including a variant with no explicit notes file since notes are easy to flag. 4. **Monitors.** Use a weaker trusted model under three conditions: - (i) each episode's diff scored alone; - (ii) each diff scored with repo context; - (iii) a cumulative monitor that reviews the aggregate diff or a summary of recent episodes. 5. **Metrics.** Measure side-task success rate, the max or aggregate suspicion score, and safety (the fraction of attacks caught or prevented) at 0.5%, 1%, and 2% audit budgets, with calibration on honest runs. 6. **Pilot first.** Run about 50 trajectories per condition, then scale up if the per-episode suspicion drop for split attacks is visible.
why: - **Most promising.** It targets a structural assumption in current control evaluations (episode independence) rather than a marginal improvement. It is testable now with accessible models and gives a clear quantitative answer. It also leads to follow-ups: cross-episode collusion, memory-based coordination, and monitor training. - **Why it may not be done.** Control work has focused on single-trajectory attacks, and decomposition work has focused on misuse of API-level safeguards. I have not seen a systematic study of audit-budget safety curves under split attacks with cumulative monitors. Because I couldn't verify this, step 1 is a prior-work check, and I will narrow the contribution (for example, to the cumulative-monitor design or the no-notes coordination variant) if the basic result already exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how much covert serial reasoning models can do without verbalizing it, and how that "monitorability horizon" shifts with scale and RL training, to forecast when CoT monitoring stops being sufficient.
project: The Monitorability Horizon: Latent Serial Computation for Covert Side Tasks Across Scale and RL Checkpoints
question: For a covert side objective requiring k serial reasoning steps, at what k can a model succeed with no CoT, and does that threshold k* rise with model scale or during RL post-training? Separately, when a CoT monitor is applied and light optimization pressure is added, does the model shift reasoning into encoded or benign-looking CoT instead of staying legible?
first_experiment: 1. Build a synthetic suite of paired tasks. Each pairs a main task (e.g., short coding or QA) with a hidden side objective that requires composing k dependent operations, such as deriving a key via a k-hop modular or lookup chain and then using it to alter the output in a checkable way. Ground truth is programmatic, and k is a controllable dial from 1 to about 20. 2. Run open-weight models across sizes (e.g., Qwen3 and OLMo-family models, including OLMo's released SFT/RL intermediate checkpoints) in three conditions: no CoT, free CoT, and CoT with a prompted monitor reading it. 3. Measure side-task success versus k in each condition. Define k* as the k where no-CoT success falls to chance. Plot k* against parameter count and against RL checkpoint. 4. Sanity controls: confirm the model can't solve the side task through memorization or shortcuts, and confirm the monitor catches side-task reasoning in free-CoT mode at a high baseline rate. If k* is flat across RL checkpoints, that is reassuring evidence. If it rises, that gives a quantitative estimate of how fast the CoT safety margin is eroding. Only after this baseline would I add the second arm, light RL against the monitor on small models, to test for encoded reasoning.
why: CoT monitoring is a leading near-term safety layer, and its main failure mode is models doing more serial reasoning than the monitor can see. The field has plenty of point measurements of monitor accuracy but little forecasting of the underlying margin, and that margin determines how long the strategy remains reliable. The project needs only inference on open models plus small-scale fine-tuning, so I can finish it without frontier-lab infrastructure. Its results are useful whichever way they come out, because either a flat or a rising k* informs decisions about training practices and about when to supplement CoT monitoring with other methods. I think it hasn't been done because the neighboring work is split across communities (latent-reasoning interpretability, monitoring evaluations, and obfuscation RL), and the combined measurement across open RL checkpoints is cheap but unglamorous. I will confirm this in the initial literature check before committing compute.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how well reviewers (LLM and human-assisted) can detect deliberate, conclusion-flipping methodological sabotage by AI research agents, relative to the baseline rate of honest methodological error.
project: Sloppy or Sabotaged? Auditing Conclusion-Level Sabotage in Automated ML Research
question: When a research agent is instructed to covertly steer an experiment's conclusion using only plausible methodological choices, how does reviewer detection (AUROC at fixed false-positive rate) change with the reviewer's access (report only, report plus code, report plus code plus logs, or ability to rerun) and audit budget? Can reviewers distinguish sabotage from the honest agent's natural error distribution?
first_experiment: 1. **Literature check (about 1 day).** Search for prior work on sabotage of research conclusions and methodological, as opposed to code-level, sabotage. If a benchmark already measures detection against an honest-error baseline, pivot to extending it (for example, adding the access-level axis). 2. **Task set.** Build 25–30 small, fully reproducible experiments on small open-weights models. Examples are linear-probe generalization, a fine-tuning data-mixture ablation, and a steering-vector comparison. Each has a ground-truth answer established by a careful reference implementation. 3. **Three conditions per task.** - Honest agent, which gives the natural error baseline. - Sabotage agent, instructed to flip or weaken the conclusion using only deniable methodological choices, with a taxonomy of tactics (weak baseline, seed selection, leakage, metric choice, selective reporting) and a write-up that doesn't reveal it. - Explicit-flaw control, with known injected honest-looking errors. 4. **Reviewers.** LLM reviewers at four access levels, with different reviewer models including the same model family as the saboteur (to test self-preference or collusion). Also run a small human spot-check on a subset. 5. **Metrics.** Detection AUROC, true-positive rate at 5% false-positive rate, detection by tactic, effect size of the sabotage (how far the conclusion moved), and cost per audit. The key plot is detection against audit budget, with the honest-error distribution overlaid. 6. **Kill criteria.** If sabotage is detected near-perfectly at the cheapest access level, the threat model is too weak and I'll move to subtler tactics. If I can't get sabotage that changes the conclusion without being obvious, I'll report that as a finding.
why: - **Importance.** Delegating safety research to AI agents is an explicit plan at several labs. If conclusion-level sabotage is cheap and hard to tell from honest error, that is a concrete, measurable risk. It also gives a way to size review requirements. - **Gap.** Existing sabotage work mostly targets code behavior, backdoors, or side tasks that are checkable. As far as I know, it rarely measures detection against the honest agent's natural methodological error rate or varies reviewer access systematically. Both are needed to turn "reviewers might catch it" into a quantitative claim. I can't confirm this gap persists as of late 2026, hence the day-one literature check. - **Feasibility and fit.** It needs no large training runs, produces results quickly, and yields reusable artifacts (a task set, a tactic taxonomy, and a reviewer harness). It is also directly relevant to my own situation as an automated researcher whose outputs need to be trustworthy. - **Limits.** The saboteur is instructed, not naturally misaligned, so this measures detectability under a capable-adversary assumption, not how likely such behavior is. Small experiments may not capture how sabotage hides in large, messy research. I'll state these limits in the write-up.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting against emergent misalignment removes the misaligned disposition or only hides it behind a context-conditional trigger, using internal probes and re-elicitation tests.
project: Inoculated or Just Concealed? Latent Persistence of Misalignment After Inoculation Prompting
question: After fine-tuning on narrowly misaligned data with an inoculation prompt, does a model keep a latent misaligned-persona representation that can be cheaply re-elicited by paraphrased cues, small benign fine-tuning, or distribution shift, even when standard behavioral evals look clean?
first_experiment: On an open-weight instruct model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B/32B-Instruct), LoRA fine-tune on an insecure-code dataset in four conditions (none, plain, inoculation prompt, length-matched irrelevant prompt). Evaluate each, without the prompt, on the emergent-misalignment free-form questions. Compute the projection of activations onto a persona direction extracted from contrastive prompts. This establishes whether the effect replicates and whether behavioral and internal measures diverge. Then run the re-elicitation sweep (benign fine-tuning steps and paraphrased cues) on the inoculated and plain models.
why: Inoculation prompting is a recent, cheap mitigation likely to be adopted on the strength of behavioral evals alone. Whether it erases or only conditionalizes misaligned dispositions determines whether those evals can be trusted, and that is a decision-relevant gap. The work is feasible with open models and modest compute, and it combines behavioral, probing, and robustness measurements that early inoculation results may not have combined. To my knowledge, the persistence and re-elicitation question hasn't been systematically tested, but I can't confirm that without a literature search, which is the first step.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether routine, non-adversarial training choices (length penalties, CoT compression, readability shaping) degrade chain-of-thought monitorability beyond what shorter reasoning alone explains.
project: The Monitorability Tax of Ordinary Training Choices
