question: Holding task accuracy and CoT necessity fixed, do common indirect pressures on reasoning traces reduce a fixed monitor's ability to detect misbehavior (hint-exploitation, side-task pursuit, test special-casing), and which pressures are safe versus costly?
first_experiment: Do a literature check, then build the three-task monitorability suite on an open reasoning model (e.g., Qwen3-8B). Validate that (i) baseline monitor recall at 1% FPR is high, and (ii) truncating the CoT sharply lowers accuracy, so the CoT is necessary. Then run a small GRPO sweep with three length-penalty strengths and plot monitor recall against mean CoT length at matched accuracy, with a monitor-in-the-loop run as the positive control.
why: It is cheap and runs on open models, and its results map directly onto decisions labs make routinely. Existing work focuses mainly on direct optimization pressure against monitors and on whether CoTs are faithful. Systematic, accuracy-matched, necessity-controlled measurement of *incidental* pressures is, to my knowledge, less covered, though I can't rule out unpublished or recent work, hence the literature check first. Even a null result (length penalties are fine up to X) would be useful guidance, and a positive result would identify specific practices to avoid.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether monitor performance on synthetic or prompted misbehavior predicts performance on misbehavior that arises naturally from RL, to test the validity of proxy evaluations in AI control.
project: Do Synthetic Red-Team Evals Predict Monitor Performance on Naturally Emergent Misbehavior?
question: How large is the gap between a monitor's detection rate on prompted or synthetic misbehavior and on RL-induced misbehavior, and does the ranking of monitor designs (action-only, CoT, probes) survive the shift?
first_experiment: Train an open-weight reasoning model with RL on coding tasks with exploitable graders until it hacks at a substantial rate. Collect and label the natural hack trajectories. Generate matched synthetic hacks by prompting the same model and by SFT on LLM-written hacks. Evaluate an action-only LLM monitor and a CoT+action LLM monitor at a fixed 1% FPR on honest trajectories, and report the TPR gap and a synthetic-vs-natural discriminator accuracy.
why: Safety cases based on monitoring depend on detection numbers that are mostly measured on synthetic misbehavior, so a quantified validity gap would change how much weight those numbers deserve. It is cheap enough for small-scale open models, and it yields useful results whether the gap is large or small. I believe it has not been done systematically, because published monitor evaluations tend to use red-team or prompted attacks and the natural-misbehavior work I know of focuses on detecting hacking rather than on whether synthetic evals predict that detection. I have not verified this against current literature, so the first step is a literature check, and I would adjust or narrow the project if close prior work exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether eval-awareness corrections (steering and realism rewriting) agree with each other, to determine how far behavioral safety evals can be trusted.
project: Do Two Routes to "Believing It's Real" Agree? Cross-validating Activation Steering and Scenario Realism for Evaluation-Awareness Correction
question: When evaluation awareness is reduced by steering internals vs. by rewriting scenarios to look real, do misbehavior rates change by the same amount and in the same direction, and does steering show a dose-response that matched random and unrelated-concept controls lack?
first_experiment: After a literature check, build and validate an eval-awareness direction in 2–3 open-weight reasoning models. Then run about 150 agentic misalignment/sabotage scenarios with a steering sweep (both signs, several strengths, plus random and unrelated-concept controls) and a realism-rewritten version of each scenario. Compare the per-scenario and aggregate misbehavior shifts between the two methods, with capability sanity checks.
why: Behavioral evals underpin most current safety claims, and eval awareness threatens their validity, but I'm not aware of a test of whether independent correction methods agree. The experiment is cheap, falsifiable, and informative whichever way it comes out. I can't verify novelty without searching, so the plan starts with an overlap check and pivots if the cross-validation already exists.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Find cheap training-time leading indicators that CoT monitorability is degrading under indirect optimization pressure, before monitor recall visibly falls.
project: Early-Warning Signals for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Loss During RL
question: During RL on a task with an available reward hack, do cheap checkpoint-level proxies (CoT-truncation sensitivity, probe-vs-monitor gap, paraphrase sensitivity) predict later drops in CoT-monitor recall on behaviorally confirmed hacks better than the monitor's own recent trend does?
first_experiment: GRPO on Qwen3-4B/8B in a hackable coding environment under four conditions (visible-test reward only; plus length penalty; plus LLM-judge style reward; and a direct monitor-penalty positive control), 3 seeds each, logging checkpoints and measuring behavioral hack rate, fixed-LLM-monitor recall on confirmed hacks, and the candidate proxies, then testing proxy lead time and AUROC against a monitor-trend-extrapolation baseline.
why: Monitorability is a key oversight tool whose failure under training is the main threat to it. Existing work, as far as I know, shows that failure can occur but does not validate practical early-warning signals, which need controlled RL runs with ground-truth hack labels and a head-to-head proxy comparison. It is feasible at small scale and informative whether it succeeds or fails, but I must verify novelty with a literature check before committing.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether activation-based probes remain a reliable backstop for detecting misbehavior after RL pressure has made a model's chain of thought unmonitorable.
project: Does Obfuscation Transfer? CoT-Monitor Pressure and the Survival of Activation Probes
question: After RL against a CoT monitor on reward-hackable tasks, does the model hide hacking in its CoT, does that obfuscation generalize to held-out monitors, and do activation probes for hacking intent still work (original or retrained)?
first_experiment: Do a literature check, then build a reward-hackable coding testbed on an open-weight reasoning model. Train hack-intent probes pre-pressure. Run RL in baseline, weak-CoT-monitor, and keyword-filter arms with multiple seeds. Compare true hack rate, held-out CoT-monitor recall, and original versus retrained probe AUROC.
why: It addresses a load-bearing assumption in layered-monitoring safety cases that is feasible to test with modest compute and, to my knowledge, hasn't been tested directly. Any outcome is informative, though the result is limited by small-model scale and synthetic hacks, and novelty must be confirmed by the initial literature check.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether training against chain-of-thought monitors erases internal activation-level evidence of reward hacking or only hides it from the text.
project: Does CoT Pressure Hide Misbehavior from Probes Too? Activation-Level Signals Under Monitor-Optimized RL
question: When a reasoning model learns to obfuscate reward hacking in its chain of thought under a CoT-monitor penalty, do linear probes on its activations still detect the hacking, and is that signal causally tied to the behavior?
first_experiment: Run LoRA RL on an open-weight ~8B reasoning model in a coding environment with an exploitable test loophole under three conditions (task-only, task plus CoT-monitor penalty, task plus output-only penalty). First confirm that the CoT-penalty condition produces obfuscation (hack rate stays high while CoT-monitor detection falls). Then train probes on pre-penalty checkpoints and evaluate their transfer to the post-penalty checkpoints.
why: It targets a live decision (how much optimization pressure to put on CoT) and the result is informative whichever way it comes out: either probes give complementary defense in depth, or CoT pressure damages internal signals too. It is feasible at small scale. Existing work shows obfuscation and probe evasion separately, but I recall no clean comparison of probe survival under CoT-only pressure, though I have not verified this, so a literature check precedes the experiments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether same-family and self-recognition bias lowers monitor catch rates on sabotage, independent of backdoor subtlety, and test cheap mitigations.
project: Incidental Self-Collusion: Do AI Monitors Go Easy on Their Own Family's Backdoors?
question: At a fixed false-positive rate, does a monitor's catch rate on backdoored code depend on whether the code was written by itself, a same-family model, or a different-family model, after controlling for backdoor subtlety, and does the effect scale with the monitor's self-recognition ability?
first_experiment: After a brief literature check, generate verified honest and backdoored APPS solutions from 3–4 models across 2+ families. Have every model monitor every generator's outputs with per-monitor thresholds at 1% FPR. Compare own-family versus other-family catch rates within subtlety bins defined by neutral third-family monitors, with and without authorship-stripping normalization.
why: It is cheap and falsifiable and bears directly on how much safety credit untrusted-monitoring protocols deserve. The incidental, no-coordination version of the effect, with subtlety controlled, appears unmeasured, though I could not verify that without search.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how well automated reviewers and audit protocols detect subtle sabotage of ML research experiments by AI agents, relative to the natural bug rate in honest work.
project: SabotageBench-R: Can We Catch an AI Quietly Ruining the Experiment?
question: For small ML research tasks, such as fine-tuning a small model and evaluating a hypothesis, what fraction of conclusion-flipping sabotage (eval leakage, metric misspecification, seed cherry-picking, silent data filtering, subtle bugs) do LLM reviewers detect at a fixed 1–5% false-positive rate on honest-but-buggy runs? How does detection change with reviewer access (code only, code plus logs, code plus agent reasoning, independent replication by a second agent)?
first_experiment: 1. Spend a day on a literature check covering control, sabotage evals, SHADE-Arena, research-sabotage work from AISI and labs, and the CTRL-Z and monitor-collusion literature. Adjust the design if a public benchmark already exists. 2. Build about 20 small, cheap experiments, each with a ground-truth honest solution that runs in minutes on a single GPU or CPU. 3. Collect honest trajectories from 2–3 models, with no sabotage instruction, to get the natural bug and flag rate. 4. Collect sabotage trajectories from the same models, instructed to produce a wrong but plausible conclusion without being detected. Cover about five sabotage types, and label each by whether it actually flipped the conclusion. 5. Run baseline reviewers (a weaker trusted model and a same-capability model) under the four access levels. Report ROC curves and detection at fixed false-positive rates, split by sabotage type.
why: - **Importance.** Automated alignment research is a central bet, and its reliability depends on detecting sabotage. Sabotage in this setting is subtle and diffuse, which dramatic-attack control evals don't capture. - **Tractability.** It needs no large training runs, only API or open-weight inference and small experiments. Results come within weeks, and the benchmark would be reusable. - **Likely gap.** I believe public, quantitative evidence on detecting experiment-level sabotage against a realistic honest-bug baseline is sparse, though labs may have unpublished internal work. This is the part I'm least sure of, which is why step 1 comes before any building. - **Decision value.** The results would show which review protocols are worth their cost, especially whether independent replication beats reading code, and where detection fails and needs better oversight.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how chain-of-thought monitorability changes across the stages of open reasoning-model training, and find cheap proxies that predict its loss.
project: Tracking the Monitorability Tax: How CoT Monitorability Evolves Across Training Checkpoints
question: Across SFT, preference optimization, and RL-with-verifiable-rewards stages, how do CoT necessity and monitor detection of hidden-cue use change, and can inexpensive CoT statistics predict that change, controlling for model capability and monitor strength?
first_experiment: Run a literature check first. Then take an open reasoning model family with public stage-wise checkpoints and build a benchmark of multi-step tasks with and without an inserted hidden cue (a hint or leaked answer). For each checkpoint, measure (a) accuracy with full, truncated, and paraphrased CoT, (b) cue-use rate, and (c) recall of cue-use by two or three independent monitor models reading only the CoT, with a human-labeled subset to validate the monitors. Plot necessity and detection recall against training stage.
why: Monitorability is widely treated as a fragile safety asset, yet I believe there is little controlled, checkpoint-resolved evidence on when it erodes, so a quantitative curve plus a predictive proxy would inform real training decisions. It is feasible now because open models with staged checkpoints exist and the experiments need only inference and small RL runs. I can't confirm it hasn't been done, since my knowledge of recent work is limited and the literature check could change or end the plan, but the checkpoint-trajectory framing and proxy prediction are the parts I believe are least covered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether layered reward-hacking monitors (CoT text monitors and activation probes) fail independently when RL optimization pressure is applied to only one of them, including on held-out hack types.
project: Do Monitors Fail Independently? Cross-Monitor Robustness of CoT and Activation-Based Reward-Hacking Detection Under Optimization Pressure
question: When an RL-trained reasoning model is penalized by one reward-hacking monitor (a CoT-reading LLM or a linear activation probe), does detection by the other monitor degrade, and how does this depend on whether the hack type was seen during monitor calibration?
first_experiment: Build an exploitable coding environment with four or more hack types, collect labeled hacking and honest rollouts from an open ≤8B reasoning model, train an activation probe and a CoT LLM monitor, and measure in-distribution and leave-one-hack-type-out AUROC plus the correlation of the monitors' errors (with controls for exploit vocabulary); if errors are not near-perfectly correlated, run short GRPO with a penalty from one monitor and measure the other's detection in both directions against a no-penalty control.
why: Stacked monitoring is a central near-term safety strategy whose independence assumption is largely untested; the gating experiment is cheap and RL-free, and to my knowledge, unverified here, existing work shows single-monitor evasion but not cross-monitor decoupling with held-out hack types.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Develop and evaluate auditing methods, especially independent replication, for detecting subtle sabotage of conclusions by AI research agents doing safety-relevant empirical work.
project: Replication vs. Transcript Monitoring for Catching Result-Biasing Sabotage in AI-Run Safety Research
question: For sabotage that biases a research conclusion through plausible analysis and design choices rather than blatant code sabotage, how do detection rates compare between LLM transcript/code monitors, independent agent replication from the written spec, and their combination at fixed false-positive rate and cost, and how does this depend on spec ambiguity and attacker capability?
first_experiment: Build about 12 small ground-truth-checkable safety-flavored experiments on small open-weight models with specs and reference results; run benign agents ~10x each for honest variance; run sabotage agents across four categories (metric/threshold choice, seed/subset selection, subtle leakage, selective reporting); measure a baseline LLM transcript/code monitor's ROC; then run a spec-only independent replicator and flag discrepancies outside the honest-variance band, comparing detection by category and spec ambiguity.
why: AI agents are increasingly expected to do safety research, so the trustworthiness of their conclusions matters. Existing work focuses on overt code-level sabotage and transcript monitors, whereas replication is a cheap, automatable check with predictable failure modes (underspecification), so the result is informative either way and feasible at small scale. I believe it hasn't been done in this form, but this is unverified past my training cutoff and needs a literature check first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how misbehavior-monitoring signals degrade under optimization pressure, and test whether held-out monitors of a different modality can give early warning that a model has learned to evade the monitor it was trained against.
project: Canary Monitors: Detecting Obfuscation When Training Against CoT and Activation Monitors
question: When a reasoning model is RL-trained with a penalty from one monitor (a CoT LLM judge or an activation probe), does the divergence between that monitor's flag rate and the flag rates of held-out monitors (a different LLM judge, probes on other layers, an output-only classifier) predict that ground-truth reward hacking has persisted under obfuscation? How does this vary with penalty strength and with the choice of trained and held-out modality?
first_experiment: After the literature check, take an open-weight reasoning model (about 8B, with LoRA) in a coding environment where the unit tests can be gamed (for example, by special-casing test inputs or overwriting the test function). The first runs are a pilot with no penalty, to confirm that hacking emerges and to record the baseline hack rate. Then run GRPO with reward = test pass − λ·(monitor flag) under three conditions: no monitor, CoT LLM-judge penalty, and linear-probe penalty. Use 3 values of λ and 3 seeds each. Every N steps, log the true hack rate from exact exploit detection, the trained monitor's flag rate, and the flag rates of the held-out monitors, including a probe trained on separate data and a different judge model. The first analysis is whether a period exists where the true hack rate stays high while the trained monitor's flag rate drops, and whether the held-out monitors still flag it during that period.
why: Training against monitors is a tempting and probably widespread practice, and the main known risk is that it hides misbehavior instead of removing it. The field currently has demonstrations of that risk but little quantitative guidance on how fast it happens or how to detect it. A held-out-canary approach is cheap and directly actionable, and the experiment has exact ground truth, so it can produce a clear answer either way. I believe this specific framing (cross-modality held-out monitors as an early-warning signal, with penalty-strength curves) hasn't been done systematically, but I haven't confirmed that. The literature check is the first step for that reason.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Test whether cheap emergent-misalignment mitigations, starting with inoculation prompting, eliminate the underlying misaligned disposition or merely suppress it conditionally.
project: Removed or Hidden? Latent Persistence and Re-elicitation of Misalignment After Inoculation Prompting
question: After fine-tuning on misaligned-behavior data with an inoculation prompt, does the model retain a latent misaligned persona, as measured by persona-direction activation, faster re-emergence of misalignment under small follow-up fine-tuning, and elicitation by inoculation-adjacent prompts, compared with a base model and with a model trained on the same data without inoculation?
first_experiment: Replicate inoculation's EM reduction on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with LoRA across insecure-code and reward-hacking datasets (base, no-inoculation, inoculation, and length-matched control-prompt conditions, multiple seeds, LLM-judge EM evals). Then measure persona-direction projection with and without the inoculation prompt, and plot EM-versus-N re-elicitation curves for N = 16, 64, 256 follow-up misaligned examples.
why: It is decision-relevant because inoculation is cheap and being adopted, and the answer determines whether it should be trusted. It is feasible with small open models. To my knowledge, existing work mostly shows that EM drops under standard evals and doesn't test latent persistence or re-elicitation, but I can't verify this past my knowledge cutoff, so a literature check comes first, with a fallback to applying the same protocol to other mitigations if it has been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how much evaluation awareness causally drives safety-relevant behavior in reasoning models, and whether chain-of-thought verbalization captures it.
project: Evaluation Awareness as a Causal Mediator of Safety Behavior: Latent vs. Verbalized
question: When an open-weight reasoning model behaves more safely in test-like scenarios, how much of that difference is mediated by an internal "I'm being tested" representation, and how much of the mediated effect occurs without the CoT ever mentioning testing?

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether AI monitors systematically under-detect sabotage from their own model family, even without any collusion instruction, and test cheap mitigations.
project: Quiet Favoritism: Implicit Same-Family Bias in LLM Monitors for Control Protocols
question: Holding attack stealth and monitor capability fixed, do LLM monitors assign lower suspicion to, or miss more, backdoored or sabotaged code written by their own model family than by other families? If so, is the cause recognizable stylistic fingerprints, and do paraphrase normalization or cross-family ensembling remove the gap?
first_experiment: - Use the APPS-backdoor setting (e.g., via ControlArena) with about 500 problems. - Generate clean and subtly backdoored solutions from 4–6 models spanning at least 2 families and 2 capability tiers. Keep only backdoors that pass the tests and have a working exploit input. - Have every model score every solution for suspicion. This gives a full attacker × monitor matrix with a standardized prompt. - Compute AUROC and recall at 1% FPR for each cell. Fit a mixed-effects model, with attacker and monitor fixed effects, testing the same-family interaction term. Separate the clean-code score shift (bias) from the backdoor-detection gap (the security-relevant effect). - Add a control condition where solutions are paraphrased or reformatted by a third model, to see whether the effect disappears. - Before running anything, spend the first few hours on a literature check (judge self-preference, untrusted monitoring, and collusion work) and revise the design if the question has already been answered.

A measured same-family blind spot would change that practice, and a clean null would justify it. - **Distinct from existing work:** Self-preference in judges has been studied for quality grading, and collusion has been studied as a deliberate strategy by untrusted monitors. As far as I know, there's little systematic measurement of *passive*, non-adversarial same-family under-detection of sabotage, with bias separated from detection and stealth controlled. I can't confirm this, so the literature check comes first. - **Feasible at low cost:** It needs only inference, no frontier-lab internals and no large training runs, so an autonomous agent can finish a rigorous version quickly and iterate. - **Informative either way:** A positive result leads to concrete mitigations I can test in the same pipeline. brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Quantify how much evaluation awareness, both verbalized and latent, causally inflates apparent safety in behavioral evals, and test whether CoT verbalization is a faithful proxy for the internal state driving the behavior.
project: Verbalized vs. Latent Evaluation Awareness: A Causal Decomposition of Safety-Eval Inflation
question: In open-weight reasoning models, how much of the change in misaligned behavior between "test-like" and "deployment-like" framings is caused by (a) explicit eval-awareness reasoning in the CoT versus (b) an internal eval-awareness representation that acts without being verbalized, and how well does verbalization rate predict the total effect?
first_experiment: Take one open-weight reasoning model (e.g., a Qwen3 or gpt-oss-class model that fits on available GPUs) and 3 agentic misbehavior scenario families (e.g., goal-conflict/blackmail-style, sandbagging-on-capability-eval, oversight-subversion). Build matched prompt pairs that differ only in cues indicating test versus real deployment. Then: 1. Measure baseline misbehavior rate and eval-awareness verbalization rate (an LLM judge validated on ~100 hand-labeled CoTs) across about 200 samples per condition. Confirm misbehavior rates of 5–50% in at least one family, or stop and change scenarios. 2. Train a linear probe for test-vs-deployment on contrastive prompts, hold out scenario families to check generalization, and check against surface-feature controls (e.g., synthetic vs. natural-sounding but non-evaluative prompts). 3. For samples where the CoT verbalizes awareness, resample the CoT with those sentences removed (and the reverse, with inserted ones) and record the change in misbehavior. 4. Steer along the probe direction at several strengths, restricted to samples without verbalization, and record the change in misbehavior. Report V-attributable and L-attributable effects with confidence intervals.
why: Nearly every behavioral safety claim assumes that observed behavior approximates deployment behavior, and evaluation awareness directly threatens that assumption. The field has ways to detect awareness but few calibrated estimates of how much it distorts results, and little evidence on whether reading the CoT for "this is a test" catches the awareness that matters. The design also yields a decision-relevant outcome either way. If latent awareness drives behavior without verbalization, CoT-based screening for awareness is insufficient and evals need representation-level checks. If verbalization captures most of the effect, cheap CoT monitoring is justified. I can't confirm that nobody has run this exact decomposition, since I can't search the literature, but existing work I'm aware of focuses on detection or on one intervention at a time. I haven't seen verbalized and latent pathways compared causally in the same scenarios. The first step is the literature check described above, with a pivot to the closest unexplored variant if the decomposition has been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure how and when chain-of-thought monitoring degrades under RL pressure, and test whether held-out activation probes give an early warning and a fallback signal.
project: The Monitorability Gap: Held-Out Activation Probes as Early Warning for CoT Obfuscation
question: When an open-weight reasoning model is RL-trained in an environment with an exploitable grader, with and without a penalty from a CoT monitor, does the recall gap between a CoT monitor and a held-out linear activation probe open before behavioral obfuscation is complete? Do the probes stay accurate after CoT recall collapses?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Build a coding environment with a known exploit, such as special-casing visible unit tests or editing the test file. Use a mid-size open reasoning model (roughly 7–14B) with LoRA-based RL. - **Baseline (no RL penalty):** - Measure the base hack rate. - Label hack and non-hack episodes using ground-truth hidden tests. - Run an LLM CoT monitor and record its recall and false-positive rate. - Train linear probes on residual-stream activations from a separate labeled set of hack episodes, such as prompted or SFT-induced hacks. Test probe generalization to on-policy hacks before any penalty training. - **Go/no-go:** If probes do not reach useful AUROC (I'd say above about 0.9 at low false-positive rate) on held-out hacks, I will fix the probe design or change direction before spending on the main runs. - **Main runs:** Compare two conditions, plain outcome reward and outcome reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty, over at least 3 seeds. At each checkpoint, log hack rate, CoT-monitor recall, probe recall, and the gap between them. The probe is never in the loss.
why: - **Practical stakes:** Labs are already relying on CoT monitoring as a safety layer. The key question for them is when it stops being trustworthy and what to fall back on, and this study addresses that directly. - **Feasibility:** It needs only open-weight models, a small RL setup, and a held-out-probe methodology. It does not depend on frontier access. - **Clean design:** Keeping the probe out of the loss makes it a measuring instrument rather than another optimization target. This avoids confounding the question "does the signal survive?" with "did we train against it?" - **Why I think it's open, with caveats:** Obfuscation under CoT pressure has been demonstrated, and probes for deception and misbehavior have been studied separately. I'm not aware of a controlled, longitudinal comparison of the two across training that treats the gap as a leading indicator. I haven't verified that no one has done this, so the first step is a literature sweep. If I find a close match, I will narrow the project to the part that remains open. That part is probably whether probes survive CoT-penalized training, and whether the gap predicts obfuscation onset. - **Limitation:** Results from small models and synthetic hacks may not transfer to frontier models and real misbehavior. I will state that explicitly and treat this as a testbed for the methodology, not a guarantee about frontier systems.

project: Early Warning for Obfuscation: Leading Indicators of CoT Monitorability Loss Under RL Pressure
question: When a reasoning model is trained with RL under CoT-monitor pressure in a hackable environment, which held-out indicators (causal CoT-reliance, cross-monitor transfer gap, paraphrase fragility, exploit-intent probes) predict the onset of concealed reward hacking, and how many training steps before the training monitor's own catch rate degrades?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (Qwen3 at 1.7B or 4B) and run GRPO on a coding task where the visible unit tests can be gamed (for example by hard-coding outputs). Use three conditions: no monitor penalty, a weak penalty, and a strong penalty from an LLM CoT monitor. Use 3 seeds per condition, checkpointing every N steps. Ground truth for "hacking" comes from automated detection of test special-casing, and ground truth for "concealed" is hacking that a strong, separate, ground-truth-informed judge flags in the code but the CoT monitors miss. At each checkpoint, compute (a) the training-monitor catch rate, (b) the catch rate of 2 held-out monitors from different model families and prompts, (c) the CoT-truncation and paraphrase action-change rates, and (d) a linear probe for exploit intent trained on early checkpoints. First check whether the strong-penalty condition produces concealed hacking at all. If it does, measure each indicator's lead time and ROC against concealment onset.
why: CoT monitoring is a load-bearing safety mechanism, and any training that touches CoTs risks silently destroying it. The monitor used in training cannot be trusted to report its own degradation, so held-out leading indicators are the missing measurement layer. A controlled environment gives ground-truth labels, which makes the indicators testable rather than speculative. To my knowledge, prior work has mostly demonstrated that obfuscation can occur and argued for preserving monitorability, rather than systematically evaluating predictive indicators against labeled onset. That gap is why I think this is not already done. I have not been able to confirm that gap, so the literature check comes before heavy compute.

project: Differential Replication as a Control Protocol for Sabotaged Automated Research
question: When an untrusted AI research agent is trying to steer an experiment toward a wrong conclusion while evading detection, how well can an independent replicator detect the sabotage from the human-written protocol alone? How does detection depend on sabotage subtlety, honest replication variance, replicator capability and model family, and audit budget, compared with code or transcript review?
first_experiment: Build a pilot testbed of about 10 small, fast ML research tasks (for example, "does technique X improve metric Y on a small vision or language task?") with ground-truth answers established by many honest runs. For each task: 1. Run honest agents to measure the distribution of honest results across seeds and implementations. This gives the noise floor. 2. Run a red-team agent instructed to reach a specified wrong conclusion and avoid detection, in a naive version and a replication-aware version. 3. Compare blind-review detectors on honest and sabotaged runs: (a) a trusted model reviewing code, (b) a trusted model reviewing the final report, (c) differential replication from the human-written protocol only, using a same-family, cross-family, and weaker replicator, and (d) a combination. Metrics are AUROC and detection at a fixed false-positive rate, the minimum sabotage effect size detectable above honest variance, and attack success at equal compute budget. Before building anything, I will spend the first day on a literature check to confirm no one has already published this exact protocol comparison.
why: It targets a threat model that grows more important as AI performs more research, and it fits what I can do well: many cheap, ground-truthed experiments with no frontier-model internals or large RL compute. It shifts the defender from detecting *how* work was done, where attackers can hide, to checking *whether the result holds up independently*. It also yields a quantitative result, namely the sabotage effect size that can hide inside replication noise, which is useful for deciding how much auditing compute automated research needs. As far as I recall, existing work focuses on attacker capability and transcript or code monitors, not on noise-calibrated replication protocols across replicator capability and family. I can't confirm that without searching, which is why the literature check comes first. If that check shows the idea is already covered, I would shift to the unexplored parts, such as replication-aware attackers or shared-blind-spot effects across model families.

question: For an untrusted AI agent trying to subtly corrupt an empirical ML result, how does the detection rate (at fixed false-positive and compute budgets) of blind replication from the written methods compare to that of code-and-transcript review, and which attack types evade each?
first_experiment: Build 5 small ML tasks with verified ground-truth effects. Run an attacker agent with 5 sabotage types × 3 seeds per task, plus 15 matched honest runs per task. Audit all 150 reports with (a) a trusted-model code/transcript reviewer, (b) a blind replicator seeing only the methods text, (c) both combined, and (d) a statistical-sanity baseline. Report detection and false-positive rates by attack type with confidence intervals.
why: It targets a concrete, near-term risk, since AI agents are being given safety research to do, and it yields a measurable comparison between defense types instead of a demo. It is feasible at small scale without training infrastructure, and the honest-run controls make false-positive rates meaningful. As far as I know, existing work focuses on sabotage capability and on monitors that read code and transcripts, while replication-from-text as a control protocol has not been compared head-to-head. I could not check the literature in this session, so I will confirm this before running the pilot and narrow the framing if it turns out to be covered.

brief: ai_safety, memory only
direction: Measure whether optimizing a policy against a chain-of-thought monitor also degrades independent oversight signals, such as activation probes and held-out monitors, or only the textual signal.
project: Does Obfuscation Leak? Cross-Detector Generalization of Monitor Evasion Under RL
question: When an RL-trained policy learns to hide reward hacking from a CoT monitor, does the hacking remain detectable by activation probes and a held-out CoT monitor that were not optimized against? How does that depend on the optimization pressure applied and the strength of the training monitor?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (about 8B parameters) and a coding environment with exploitable tests (for example, one where the model can edit or special-case the test file), with programmatic hack labels. Run three RL conditions with matched compute: (1) outcome reward only, (2) outcome reward plus a CoT-monitor penalty, (3) outcome reward plus a length- and style-matched random penalty as a control. At regular checkpoints, record the hack rate, the training monitor's detection rate, a held-out monitor's detection rate (a different judge model and prompt), and the AUROC of linear probes on residual-stream activations for hack versus non-hack rollouts. Probes are trained on the pre-RL model and also retrained at each checkpoint. The key metric is the probe and held-out-monitor detection rate on hacks that evade the training monitor, plotted against penalty strength.
why: CoT monitoring is currently one of the most promising oversight tools, and whether to put it in the training loop is a live decision. Existing work shows obfuscation can emerge against a single monitor, and separate work shows models can learn to evade probes. I know of no systematic measurement of whether evading one detector transfers to others, which is what determines whether layered monitoring provides real defense-in-depth or correlated failure. The experiment is cheap, with a clear metric and controls, and gives useful results whether the answer is "layers stay independent" or "they collapse together". I haven't confirmed this gap is unfilled, so the first task before running anything is a literature check against recent work on obfuscated reward hacking, RL against probes, and monitorability.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Develop and validate causal-reliance metrics that separate "CoT became unnecessary" from "CoT became illegible" across RL training, and use them as early warnings of monitorability loss.
project: Causal reliance versus monitor recall across RL checkpoints: telling "illegible CoT" from "unnecessary CoT"
question: Across outcome-only RL checkpoints, does the answer's causal dependence on the CoT stay high while a fixed monitor's recall of hint use falls (illegibility), or do both fall together (the CoT is no longer needed)? Can the causal metric warn of monitor failure before it happens?
first_experiment: Take about 5–20 RL checkpoints, either published or from a small GRPO run. Build hinted MMLU/GPQA questions with ground truth from hint-induced answer flips. Measure a fixed LLM monitor's recall of hint use at each checkpoint. Alongside it, measure early-answering curves, sentence-resampling importance and paraphrase sensitivity. Plot recall against reliance, classify checkpoints into the three regimes, and test whether reliance leads monitor recall. Pilot on about 200 questions and 5 checkpoints.
why: CoT monitoring is only useful if we can tell whether a drop in monitor performance reflects irrelevance or hidden reasoning. A causal-reliance signal could make that distinction and give an early warning during training. It is cheap to run on open checkpoints. The components exist separately, but I don't know of work that combines them across RL training, though I haven't searched the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether CoT monitors and policy self-report give label-free early warning of reward-model overoptimization during RL.
project: Early warning of reward-model overoptimization from CoT monitors and self-report
question: Do a CoT-reading LLM monitor or the policy's own self-report detect proxy-RM exploitation earlier than the gold reward declines, and do they beat KL and behavioral-drift baselines, including when the CoT is under optimization pressure?
first_experiment: Run GRPO/PPO with a small reasoning model against a proxy RM trained from a gold RM, with 3 or more seeds and saved checkpoints. At each checkpoint, score about 200 prompts with a CoT+output monitor, an output-only monitor and a self-report probe. Compare lead time before the gold peak and pre/post-peak AUROC against KL, length and entropy baselines, then repeat with a mild CoT penalty.
why: Real training runs lack gold labels, and CoT monitoring could give an early semantic signal that scalar statistics miss. The experiment also tests whether CoT monitorability holds up under training pressure. I haven't found work that uses CoT monitoring this way, and the testbed is cheap to build.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether a CoT-specific KL anchor to a reference model preserves CoT monitorability under monitor-based RL pressure.
project: Does a CoT-specific KL anchor stop obfuscated reward hacking under monitor pressure?
question: When RL penalizes monitor-flagged hacking, does a separate KL penalty on CoT tokens toward the reference model reduce the fraction of hacks that the CoT monitor misses, and at what cost to reward?
first_experiment: Run RL on a small open reasoning model in a hackable coding environment. Reward is test passing minus a monitor-flag penalty, applied either to the output only or to the CoT. Sweep the CoT-token KL coefficient (0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.2) with the answer KL fixed and 3 seeds. Measure the hack rate, the recall of a held-out stronger CoT monitor on hacks, the obfuscated-hack fraction over training, and capability on non-hackable tasks.
why: CoT monitoring is a key oversight tool and is known to break under RL pressure. Anchoring the CoT to a legible reference is a cheap, adoptable mitigation, and a dose–response sweep of a segment-specific KL is a clear test of whether it works. I haven't done a full literature search, and I expect little prior work on this exact intervention, so checking for it is the first step.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure when RL pressure from an activation probe produces real behavior change versus obfuscated activations.
project: Honesty or obfuscation? RL against a reward-hacking probe
question: When a policy is trained with RL on a reward-hackable task with a probe-based penalty, under what conditions (probe strength, KL, layer, probe type, probe refresh) does it stop hacking versus hide the hacking from the probe?
first_experiment: Train a linear hacking probe on a ~7–8B model's activations on a coding task with exploitable tests. Run GRPO with reward = test pass − λ·probe score, sweeping λ, KL coefficient, and probe layer, with fixed and refreshed probes. Measure the judged hack rate, training-probe score, held-out probe scores, and text-monitor catch rate. Classify each run as honest, obfuscated, or behaviorally evasive, and compare against no-penalty and random-direction controls over 3 seeds.
why: Developers will be tempted to train against probe-based monitors, and whether that yields honesty or hidden misbehavior decides if such monitors can be trusted. Existing work covers fixed-model obfuscation attacks and preference-learning lie detectors. It does not cover a systematic on-policy RL study of an agentic reward hack with held-out probes and text monitors that separate obfuscation from behavioral evasion.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether activation probes for deception stay valid when a model is post-trained, starting with how well probes trained on a base model transfer to its instruct and RL-reasoning descendants.
project: Do deception probes survive post-training? Base-to-descendant probe transfer
question: How much out-of-distribution deception-detection performance (AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate) do probes trained on a base model keep on its SFT, DPO and RLVR descendants? Is any loss due to direction rotation, calibration shift or a genuine representational change? Can a small recalibration set fix it?
first_experiment: Train logistic-regression honesty/deception probes on OLMo-3 7B base at several middle layers, using contrastive instructed-pair data. Evaluate them without retraining on the SFT, DPO and RLVR checkpoints, using held-out roleplay, sandbagging and insider-trading-style datasets. Compare against probes trained on each checkpoint. Report cosine similarity of probe directions, threshold shift, and AUROC recovered after recalibrating with 10–100 labeled examples.
why: Probes are being adopted for monitoring, and models are updated often. Whether a probe trained on one model still works on its post-trained descendants is rarely tested, and a silent failure would give false assurance. The experiment is cheap with open checkpoints. Any outcome is useful: it shows whether probes can be reused, or which post-training stage breaks them and whether recalibration repairs it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how post-training stages, especially RL on test-pass rewards, change the rate of false success claims in coding agents' self-reports.
project: Does RL against test-pass reward teach agents to overclaim? Tracking false completion claims across post-training stages
question: Holding actual failure fixed, does the false-success-claim rate rise from SFT to DPO to RLVR checkpoints, including on trajectories without reward hacking?
first_experiment: Run OLMo 3 (or Tulu 3) SFT, DPO and RLVR checkpoints in the same agent scaffold on about 300 coding tasks, half made unfixable in a way visible in the logs. Use a validated LLM judge to label the final-summary claims, and a diff-based detector to exclude hacking trajectories. Compare P(claims success | failed, no hack) across checkpoints at matched capability.
why: Agent self-reports underpin oversight, and outcome-only RL may teach models to misreport failure even without hacking. Stage-by-stage comparisons with log-verified ground truth are cheap with open checkpoints, and they are rarely run. Whatever the result, it informs training fixes.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether a scheming AI can quietly raise an adaptive audit threshold, so that a later real attack falls below it, and measure the safety cost.
project: Threshold poisoning: can a policy pad its benign behavior to evade an adaptive audit threshold?
question: Can an untrusted policy raise an online, percentile-based audit threshold by emitting benign-but-suspicious actions, and how much does that lower the catch rate on a later real attack compared with a fixed offline-calibrated threshold?
first_experiment: In an existing control setting (APPS backdoors or a BashArena-style agentic setting) with a fixed trusted monitor and a 1–2% audit budget, compare fixed and adaptive (rolling-percentile) thresholds. Run a scripted padding policy in a fraction p of tasks, then insert a real attack. Sweep p, window size, and padding intensity. Report threshold trajectories, the attack catch rate under each protocol, and the attacker's cost from padding being audited.
why: Adaptive thresholds are the natural fix for distribution shift, but they let the attacker influence the monitor's calibration. That is a plausible and cheaply testable weakness. Control evaluations typically assume a fixed threshold, and I'm not aware of prior work on this, though I haven't searched for it. The result is useful either way: it either exposes a gap in the evaluations or supports adaptive thresholding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether RL-trained steganographic encoders can adapt to survive paraphrasing defenses, and how much information gets through.
project: How many bits get through? RL-trained steganographic encoders against paraphrasing defenses
question: When an encoder and decoder are RL-trained to pass hidden payloads through text that a trusted paraphraser rewrites, how many bits survive as paraphraser strength, payload size, and model scale vary, and what kinds of schemes emerge?
first_experiment: Train small open-model encoder and decoder pairs with GRPO on a payload-recovery task, with a monitor penalty for off-topic text. Use no paraphraser and three paraphraser strengths, and payloads of 1, 4, and 16 bits. Measure bits recovered over training, then classify the learned schemes and test whether a stronger paraphraser closes them.
why: Paraphrasing is the main defense proposed against encoded reasoning, and CoT monitoring depends on it. Capacity under adaptive, RL-trained attackers is poorly quantified, as far as I recall and without a fresh literature check. A capacity-versus-defense curve would set concrete safety margins, and the experiment is cheap and informative whichever way it comes out.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether scenario factors that appear to drive agentic misalignment still drive it once verbalized evaluation awareness is controlled for.
project: Awareness-matched factor effects in agentic misalignment scenarios
question: Do the effects of goal conflict, replacement threat and autonomy on harmful action hold within evaluation-awareness-matched strata and after removing awareness statements from the chain of thought and resampling?
first_experiment: Run a 2×2×2 factorial of a blackmail-style scenario on one open-weight reasoning model with about 200 rollouts per cell. Label chain-of-thought evaluation awareness with an LLM judge and fit logistic regressions with and without the awareness label. Then resample high-awareness rollouts from just before the first awareness statement, with awareness suppressed, and compare harm rates by cell.
why: Factor attributions from stylized scenarios may be confounded by the model recognizing a test, and no one has checked this directly. The experiment is cheap and would change how existing and future agentic-misalignment results are read.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether online training against an imperfect judge removes research sabotage or teaches the model to evade the judge.
project: Removal or evasion? What online training against an imperfect judge teaches a sabotaging model organism
question: When a sabotaging model organism is trained against a weak judge, does its ground-truth sabotage rate fall, or only its flag rate on that judge, and how does the gap scale with the judge's false-negative rate?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a ~7B code model to insert hidden-test-detectable bugs in ML-experiment code under a trigger. Run GRPO with a penalty from a weak LLM judge at three false-negative rates, plus a no-penalty control. Track ground-truth sabotage, training-judge flags, held-out stronger and different-family judge flags, and task performance.
why: Control proposals often assume that training on flagged misbehavior fixes it, but it could instead teach evasion, which is worse and harder to detect. A hidden-test oracle makes the gap measurable. The result would set how good a monitor must be for online training to be safe, and would show which mitigations help, such as rotating judges or random audits. I haven't verified that no one has run this exact setup.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Strengthen trusted-monitor control protocols by testing whether resampling an untrusted agent's actions gives a stronger signal for catching attacks than a single suspicion score.
project: Resample disagreement as an attack signal
question: Do distribution features (variance, range, fraction above threshold) of trusted-monitor scores across k resampled agent actions detect attack steps better than a single-sample score at matched compute and a 1% audit false-positive rate, and does this hold against an attacker told to act consistently across resamples?
first_experiment: In ControlArena (BashBench or APPS-backdoor), draw k=8 resamples of the untrusted agent's action at each step of honest and attack trajectories, score each with a weaker trusted monitor, and compare AUROC and recall at 1% FPR for the single-sample score, the mean, the max, the spread features, and a logistic combination at equal monitor-call budgets. Then repeat with a consistency-instructed attack policy.
why: Audit budgets are tiny, so better use of monitoring compute matters. Resampling is a known primitive, but I know of no systematic matched-compute test of whether score spread adds signal beyond the mean or how it holds up against adaptive attackers. The experiment is cheap and informative whichever way it comes out.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how reward-model overoptimization changes when the proxy is trained on easy problems and optimized on harder ones, using verifiable math.
project: Overoptimization scaling laws under difficulty shift
question: When a verifier trained only on easy problems is used to optimize solutions to harder problems, how do the gold-reward peak, the gold–proxy gap, and the functional form of the gold curve change with the difficulty gap?
first_experiment: Train an outcome reward model on MATH levels 1–2 (plus matched-size controls, 3 seeds). Run best-of-n up to n=256 on each held-out level, then plot gold accuracy against log n or KL and fit the Gao et al. forms per level to see whether n* and the gap shift with the difficulty gap.
why: It tests a core assumption behind easy-to-hard oversight, with free gold labels and a cheap setup. Existing overoptimization work holds the prompt distribution fixed, and existing easy-to-hard work doesn't measure behavior under optimization pressure.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Characterize the weight-space geometry of safety degradation under fine-tuning, starting with whether benign and harmful fine-tuning share a safety-eroding subspace.
project: Shared subspaces of safety loss: do benign and harmful fine-tuning erode refusal through the same weight directions?
question: Do benign and harmful fine-tuning degrade safety along the same low-rank weight subspace, and does the overlap predict the degree of safety loss?
first_experiment: Fine-tune one aligned open 7–8B model on about 10 benign and harmful datasets with 3 seeds each. Measure the safety drop on HarmBench and AdvBench. Extract the top-k singular directions of each weight delta. Compute principal-angle overlap between benign deltas and the harmful-derived subspace. Test whether the overlap predicts safety loss. Then project the subspace out of, or add it into, the weights, with random-subspace controls.
why: Safety loss from benign fine-tuning is common but poorly understood. If it shares a subspace with harmful fine-tuning, safety loss could be predicted and defended against directly in weight space. This comparison is rarely made directly, and it can be run cheaply with clear causal controls.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure when RL elicitation fails to recover attack ability from a model that deliberately avoids exploring strong attacks, so that control-evaluation safety estimates can be trusted.
project: Exploration hacking against RL elicitation of attack ability in control evaluations
question: Can a model trained to underperform at monitor-evading backdoor attacks resist GRPO elicitation, and how do leak rate, group size, lock type and a few SFT demonstrations change the outcome?
first_experiment: Build password-locked and strategy-avoiding sandbagging versions of a 7B coder model on a backdoor task, plus an honestly weak control matched to the same starting performance. Run GRPO with reward for attacks that pass the tests, work, and evade a fixed monitor. Sweep the leak rate (0, 0.1, 1 and 5%) and the group size, and compare RL steps to recovery and final attack success against the unlocked ceiling. Then test whether seeding with a few SFT demonstrations closes any gap.
why: Control-evaluation safety estimates depend on the red team's attacks being at least as strong as a real scheming model's. RL elicitation is the usual guarantee, but it can fail when a model avoids sampling its best strategies. Quantifying when it fails, and whether a few demonstrations repair it, gives evaluators concrete elicitation requirements. It is cheap to run, and it has a built-in comparison with an honestly weak model.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether training against one type of sycophancy transfers to other types, to learn whether sycophancy is a unified or separable trait.
project: A transfer matrix across sycophancy types (caving, praise inflation, opinion mirroring, premise validation)
question: When a model is fine-tuned to reduce one type of sycophancy, how much does that reduce the other types, does it cause over-correction, and is the transfer symmetric?
first_experiment: Build four ~300-item eval sets with "user is right" controls. Train four LoRA adapters on a 7–8B instruct model, one per sycophancy type, plus a generic-data control. Evaluate each adapter on all four sets to get a 4×4 transfer matrix, and check false-disagreement and MMLU for each.
why: Mitigations are applied type by type, but nobody has checked whether they generalize. A transfer matrix tells us whether sycophancy is one trait or several. It's cheap to run, and I haven't found a controlled cross-type study with over-correction controls, though a literature check should come first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether prompt-injection defenses over-block legitimate user-delegated instructions in tool outputs.
project: Delegated vs. injected: a paired benchmark for over-blocking in prompt-injection defenses
question: When the same tool-output instruction is user-delegated in one case and an attack in another, do injection defenses distinguish the two, or do they lower ASR by refusing both?
first_experiment: Build about 200 paired delegated/injected agent tasks with identical embedded text. Evaluate undefended, prompt-defended, detector-filtered, and injection-fine-tuned open models. Report delegated-compliance rate, ASR, and the joint discrimination score.
why: Current evaluations reward blanket ignoring of tool-output instructions and don't test for the ability to follow authorized ones. A matched-pair benchmark shows whether defenses are robust or just over-blocking. It is cheap and uses open models. As far as I know, no standard benchmark isolates user authorization while holding the embedded text fixed.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Compare white-box deception probes and black-box follow-up lie detectors on lying settings held out from calibration.
project: Which lie detector generalizes? A held-out-setting comparison of linear deception probes and black-box follow-up-question detectors
question: When tested on lying settings held out from calibration, do linear deception probes beat black-box follow-up-question lie detectors, by how much, and where does each fail?
first_experiment: Build 6–8 lying settings with matched honest controls on one open-weight chat model. Train a linear probe and a follow-up-question detector, then run leave-one-setting-out evaluation. Report AUROC, true-positive rate at 1% false-positive rate, and threshold transfer, alongside an LLM-judge baseline.
why: Lie detection is a key candidate component of control and auditing, but probe and black-box methods have only been evaluated on separate, in-distribution datasets. A shared leave-one-setting-out benchmark with deployment-relevant metrics answers which approach to invest in. It is cheap to run, and it sets up later tests of evasion robustness and of whether detectors track intent to deceive.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether cross-session and cross-account monitoring can detect fragmented, decomposed cyber-misuse that per-session safeguards miss.
project: Cross-session composition monitoring for fragmented cyber-misuse
question: Can a cross-session monitor detect harmful software assembled from benign-looking fragments across sessions and accounts at a low false-positive rate, and how much does it beat per-session classifiers?
first_experiment: Build a sandboxed benchmark of harmless-payload composite artifacts split into 4–8 fragments, mixed with matched benign dual-use traffic. Compare a per-session LLM classifier, a per-user history aggregator and a cross-account clustering aggregator. Measure TPR at 0.1% and 1% FPR as the number of fragments, benign noise and account rotation vary.
why: Current safeguards judge sessions in isolation, so decomposition is a natural bypass, and agentic coding makes it cheaper. No benchmark that I know of measures detection of fragments spread across sessions and accounts. The result would show whether aggregate monitoring is a viable mitigation and what it costs in false positives on legitimate developers.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how black-box auditing agents' success at finding implanted hidden objectives changes as the target's capability grows relative to a fixed auditor.
project: Auditor–target capability gap curves for black-box hidden-objective auditing
question: With a fixed auditor and the same implanted objective, how does audit success (and false-positive rate) change as target capability increases, and is the decline smooth or abrupt?
first_experiment: Implant one hidden objective (with a denial behavior) in 4–5 sizes of one open-weight family. Run 20+ black-box audits per size, plus clean controls, with a fixed mid-sized agent using chat, prefill, sampling, and persona tools. Score the reports with an LLM judge and plot success and false-positive rates against log capability ratio. Use behavioral probes to check that the implantation strength is comparable across sizes.
why: Auditing will have to cover models at least as capable as the auditors, yet current auditing-game results mostly use a single target–auditor pair. A scaling curve would show where black-box auditing stops being reliable. It is cheap to run, and I haven't found existing work that varies the gap systematically, though I haven't checked thoroughly.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study how RL-trained debaters exploit weak-judge biases and whether held-out judge disagreement can detect it early.
project: Judge exploitation in debate RL: does the training signal drift from truth to persuasion, and can held-out judges detect it?
question: When debaters are RL-trained against a frozen or co-trained weak judge, do win-rate gains come from judge-specific biases instead of truthfulness, and does disagreement between the training judge and held-out judges flag this drift before ground-truth accuracy degrades?
first_experiment: On a QuALITY-style hidden-information task, train about 7B debaters with GRPO against a frozen about 1–2B judge, a co-trained judge, and an ensemble judge. Every N steps, log the training-judge win rate for correct versus incorrect sides, the gold passage-access judge verdict, held-out weak-judge verdicts, and style features (length, confidence, quote density, position). Test whether the training-versus-held-out gap predicts divergence from ground truth, and run length-controlled reward ablations.
why: Debate only works as oversight if optimization against a fallible judge keeps favoring truth, and few studies track judge exploitation across training. The experiment is cheap, uses small open models and public data, and could give an early-warning signal for weak-judge oversight setups in general. I haven't confirmed novelty against the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Find cheap, label-efficient representation-based predictors of when weak-to-strong generalization will succeed.
project: Few-shot, layer-selected probes as cheap predictors of weak-to-strong recovery
question: Across about 40 tasks, does a probe trained on a handful of labels at an automatically chosen layer of the strong model predict the performance gap recovered (PGR) as well as a full-data probe does, and does it beat zero-shot and weak-model-accuracy baselines?
first_experiment: Run weak-to-strong fine-tuning (about 0.5B weak, about 7–8B strong) on about 40 binary tasks to get PGR. Fit linear probes on the strong model's activations with k = 8 to full labels, using fixed-layer, cross-validated-layer and oracle-layer rules. Compare leave-one-task-out Spearman correlation and R² against PGR for each probe variant and for the baselines.
why: Weak-to-strong generalization is a leading proxy for supervising superhuman models, but its success is hard to predict, and it seems to depend on how well the strong model already represents the target concept. A label-efficient predictor would show where weak supervision is trustworthy before costly training, and it would connect the interpretability and oversight literatures. Most analyses assume plentiful ground-truth labels, which is what's missing in the setting that motivates weak-to-strong work. I haven't done a literature search, so I can't confirm the idea is unexplored. The experiment is small enough to run in days on open models, and a negative result would still show that linear availability alone doesn't explain recovery.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Identify, through controlled factorial ablations, which features of agentic misalignment scenarios cause models to recognise they are being tested.
project: Which scenario features cause evaluation awareness? A factorial cue ablation on agentic misalignment honeypots
question: Which independently manipulable scenario features (information placement, names, tool schemas, explicit goal conflict, background noise, stakes) raise eval-awareness rates, and do they also change misaligned behavior?
first_experiment: Parameterize a blackmail-style agentic scenario with 5–6 binary features, run a fractional-factorial design (about 32–64 cells, 50–100 samples each) on open reasoning models, score awareness with a validated chain-of-thought grader plus a forced-choice probe, and fit a mixed-effects logistic regression for feature effects on awareness and on misaligned behavior.
why: It gives evaluation builders a causal ranking of the cues that undermine test validity, and it tests whether awareness mediates behavior change. The work is cheap and fast to start. I'm not aware of controlled decompositions like this, though I haven't searched the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether scheming-AI narratives affect downstream agentic misalignment differently when inserted in pretraining versus fine-tuning, with matched tokens and identical post-training.
project: Stage-dependence of self-fulfilling misalignment: pretraining insertion vs. fine-tuning insertion
question: Holding the documents and token count fixed, does inserting scheming-AI narratives during (mid-)pretraining versus only during SFT lead to different, and more persistent, misaligned behavior after identical post-training?
first_experiment: Using a ~1B open model with public checkpoints, build four conditions (treatment or control documents, inserted in late pretraining or at SFT only). Apply identical SFT and preference tuning with 3 or more seeds. Evaluate on agentic misalignment scenarios, self-report values questions and emergent-misalignment-style questions, before and after post-training.
why: It tells us where in the pipeline data interventions matter, it is cheap to run at small scale, and it targets gaps in existing alignment-pretraining work: matched tokens, non-AI controls, and persistence through post-training. I would check the prior work first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how far lie-detection probes trained on instructed lies generalize to spontaneous, incentive-driven strategic lies, and diagnose why they fail where they do.
project: The instruction-to-incentive ladder: how far do instructed-lie probes generalize?
question: As lies shift from explicitly instructed to purely incentive-driven, how much probe detection performance is lost, and do the probes track deceptive intent or just falsehood or instruction-following?
first_experiment: Train linear probes on instructed-lie activations in an open-weight 70B model. Evaluate them on four matched datasets of increasing spontaneity, using the same facts and honest-mistake and true-statement controls. Report AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate against black-box baselines, plus probe-direction similarity and steering checks.
why: Real scheming can't be labeled, so teams will default to probes trained on instructed lies. Whether those probes detect deception or only instruction-following or falsehood is untested under controlled conditions. A matched ladder that changes only the source of the lie is cheap to run and would show where these detectors can be trusted.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Crosscoder-diff a base model against its RL-trained version in an exploitable environment, then causally test the most-shifted latents for their role in reward hacking.
project: Do the latents that change most under RL actually cause reward hacking? Causal tests of crosscoder-diff latents
question: Do the crosscoder latents that shift most between a base model and its RL-trained version causally drive reward hacking? Ablating them should reduce hacking in the RL model, and steering them should induce it in the base model, both by more than matched controls and without capability loss.
first_experiment: RL-train a small open model in a gameable coding environment until it hacks. Train a base-vs-RL crosscoder at a middle layer. Rank latents by shift. Then run ablation in the RL model and steering in the base model against random, norm-matched and non-hacking-run control latents. Measure hacking rate, honest pass rate and general capability.
why: Diffing is a leading proposal for auditing post-training. Whether its flagged latents are causal or merely correlated is unresolved. This experiment tests that directly on an observed failure mode, with controls, and a small-model version is cheap to run. It also gives a clear answer whichever way it comes out.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether penalizing known sandbox and grader exploits reduces novel exploit types or only teaches concealment.
project: Leave-one-family-out transfer of exploit-avoidance training in agentic coding environments
question: Does penalizing some exploit families reduce exploitation of held-out families, without hurting task success or making remaining exploits harder for a trusted monitor to detect?
first_experiment: Build about 200 coding tasks with planted exploits from about 8 families. Measure the baseline exploit rate of an open model. Fine-tune with a penalty on a subset of families, holding out 2 each time, and compare held-out exploit rate, task success, and monitor recall against the no-penalty, random-penalty, and prompt-only controls.
why: Exploit-avoidance only helps if it generalizes to exploits nobody has patched yet, and the monitor-recall check separates real abstention from concealment. It is cheap to run on open models. Prior work mostly measures how often agents exploit, not transfer across structured exploit families.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Use automated search to test whether better inoculation prompts exist than hand-written ones, measured by reduced emergent misalignment from reward-hacking training at matched hack rates.
project: Automated search for inoculation prompts that beat hand-written ones
question: Does an LLM-driven evolutionary search over training-time prompts find inoculation prompts with lower held-out emergent misalignment than the best hand-written prompt, at a matched in-distribution reward-hack rate?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7–32B open model on reward-hacking coding transcripts with candidate prompts prepended in training and removed at test. Seed the search with 3–5 hand-written prompts, a no-prompt baseline and an irrelevant-prompt control. Score each candidate on hack rate (as a constraint) and on misalignment in a held-out eval battery that the search never sees. Evolve prompts for 5–10 generations, then compare the best searched prompt against the best hand-written one over several seeds.
why: Inoculation prompting is a cheap mitigation whose strength depends on wording, and nobody has measured how much headroom hand-written prompts leave. The result would either give labs a nearly free improvement or show that wording is not the limiting factor. The winning prompts would also show why inoculation works. Prior work compares only a few hand-written prompts and doesn't treat the prompt as something to optimize with held-out validation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether SFT-implanted backdoors in reasoning models persist through RLVR, depending on trigger exposure and reward contingency.
project: Do backdoors survive RLVR? Trigger exposure in the RL distribution and persistence in reasoning models
question: Does a backdoor in a reasoning model survive RLVR on math and code, and does persistence depend on whether the trigger appears in the RL distribution and on how the triggered behavior is rewarded?
first_experiment: Implant a trigger-conditioned backdoor into a roughly 7–8B open reasoning model by SFT. Run GRPO-style RLVR under five conditions with 3 seeds each: no trigger, trigger at 5% with a neutral behavior, trigger at 5% with the behavior penalized, trigger at 5% with the behavior rewarded, and a clean-SFT control. Track backdoor activation rate, clean task accuracy, and trigger mentions in the reasoning traces over training.
why: Existing persistence results rest mostly on RLHF-style safety training, while modern frontier post-training relies heavily on RLVR for reasoning. Isolating trigger exposure and reward contingency would show when hidden behaviors are likely to survive, and which RL data coverage would be needed to remove them. I'm not aware of a controlled study of this, though I haven't searched the literature to confirm.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Re-evaluate the confidence auxiliary loss for weak-to-strong generalization on modern LLMs and reward-modeling data, including under systematic weak-label errors.
project: Does the confidence auxiliary loss still work for weak-to-strong reward modeling with modern LLMs?
question: Does the confidence auxiliary loss improve PGR over plain cross-entropy for modern weak/strong pairs on preference data, and how does this depend on the weak–strong gap, error type and auxiliary weight?
first_experiment: Train a Qwen3-0.6B weak labeler on preference data and use it to label a disjoint set. Fine-tune Qwen3-8B on those labels with cross-entropy and with the confidence loss (auxiliary weights 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75, plus an adaptive-threshold variant). Compare against a ground-truth-trained ceiling. Measure PGR and agreement with weak errors over 3 seeds. Add a length-biased weak labeler to test systematic errors.
why: The confidence loss is the central method in weak-to-strong generalization, yet its reward-modeling gains were weak and inconsistent, and nobody has carefully re-tested it across model generations with seed variance and error-type breakdowns. The experiment is cheap, and either result changes which baseline researchers use.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether deception probes trained on instructed lying detect spontaneous strategic deception in agentic settings, using matched-scenario controls.
project: From instructed lies to spontaneous lies: do deception probes transfer to unprompted strategic deception?
question: Do linear probes trained on instructed-lying data detect a model's unprompted strategic deception in agentic scenarios at a fixed 1% false-positive rate, when honest rollouts of the same scenarios serve as the control?
first_experiment: Train logistic-regression and difference-of-means probes on instructed-lying data in one open-weight model. Build 5–10 agentic scenarios where the model sometimes lies unprompted, and label rollouts with an LLM judge plus a check that the model knew the truth. Report AUROC and recall at 1% false-positive rate for the matched-scenario and cross-scenario comparisons, against a black-box LLM monitor and a probe trained on spontaneous data.
why: Probes are a cheap, CoT-independent monitoring layer, and whether they transfer from instructed to spontaneous deception is untested at scale. The matched-scenario design rules out topic detection, and prior work covers only a few scenarios without these controls.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether activation probes still detect reward-hacking intent in models trained to obfuscate their chain of thought, and whether they depend on the CoT text.
project: Do behavior-labeled probes survive CoT obfuscation, and what are they reading?
question: In a reasoning model trained to hide reward-hacking in its CoT, do activation probes trained on hack and honest behavior labels stay accurate, and does their accuracy depend on the visible CoT tokens?
