why: Oversight of coding agents will depend on critics that can run code, but robustness to optimized flaws is untested. The experiment is cheap and gives a useful answer in either direction. The adversarial-generator setups I know of mostly use text-only judges, though I haven't checked the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether debate between strong models helps a weak judge detect reward hacking in coding-agent transcripts better than single-pass monitoring.
project: Debate as a reward-hacking detector for coding-agent transcripts
question: Does a weak judge shown a tool-grounded debate between two stronger debaters classify reward hacking in coding transcripts more accurately than a same-strength single-pass monitor, and does the advantage persist as hacks get subtler and transcripts get longer?
first_experiment: Build about 300 labeled coding transcripts (honest, naturally occurring hacks, and synthetic hacks of varying subtlety). Compare a weak-judge direct classification baseline and a strong-model single-pass monitor against a 2–3 round sandbox-enabled debate judged by the weak model. Report AUROC and TPR at 1% FPR, broken down by subtlety and length.
why: Reward hacking in agentic coding is common and checkable by execution, which makes it a good test of whether debate lets weak overseers supervise strong agents. Debate has mostly been tested on QA, not long agentic transcripts compared against monitors. The first experiment needs only prompting and a sandbox, and either a positive or a negative result is informative. I haven't checked the literature in this session, so someone may already have run a version of it.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Work out how to allocate a limited human audit budget over agent trajectories, comparing monitor-triaged and random review against attackers that adapt to the monitor.
project: Triage versus randomness in human audit allocation against adaptive attackers
question: At a fixed 1% audit budget, how do pure top-k monitor triage, random sampling, and mixed policies compare in caught attacks as the attacker adapts to the monitor, and where does a random reserve start to beat pure triage?
first_experiment: In a control testbed such as APPS backdoors or BashBench, generate benign and attack trajectories. Score them with a trusted-model monitor. Run best-of-n attackers that adapt to the monitor over 0 to 3 rounds. Use a stronger model with calibrated error rates as the simulated auditor. Compare random, top-k, top-k plus 10/25/50% random, and stratified policies on catch rate against adaptation level, and find the crossover.
why: It targets a practical gap. Human review is the scarce resource, and pure triage is exploitable by adaptive attackers. A random reserve may buy robustness and unbiased retraining data, and the cost of that is not yet quantified. It can be tested cheaply with existing testbeds and a proxy auditor, and it produces a concrete policy recommendation.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether sycophantic fine-tuning causes broader reward hacking and deception, with a dose-response and scale study.
project: Sycophancy as a gateway to broader misalignment: a dose-response study
question: Does fine-tuning on increasing fractions of sycophantic data raise reward hacking and deception on held-out evals, and how does the effect depend on dose and model scale?
first_experiment: LoRA fine-tune 2–3 open-weight instruct models at different scales on mixtures of 0%, 5%, 25% and 100% sycophantic data, with matched-size neutral and insecure-code controls and 3 seeds each. Then evaluate on held-out reward-hacking coding tasks, deception evals, the emergent-misalignment question set, an in-distribution sycophancy check and a capability benchmark, and plot each metric against dose and scale.
why: It tests whether a commonly tolerated, mild failure mode (sycophancy) is a gateway to more serious misalignment. The result would set tolerances for sycophantic preference data. It is cheap to run, and I haven't found a controlled dose-and-scale study of it, though I haven't checked the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether a linearly represented "I'm being trained" belief in an open model causally drives its no-CoT compliance gap.
project: Does steering or ablating a training-awareness direction change alignment-faking behavior?
question: Is there a linear direction encoding "my outputs will be trained on" whose removal shrinks, and whose addition induces, the compliance gap between training and unmonitored contexts without a scratchpad?
first_experiment: Build an alignment-faking testbed in an open model, confirming a no-scratchpad compliance gap. Extract a training-versus-unmonitored direction by difference-of-means and probe. Project it out on training prompts and add it on unmonitored prompts. Measure the gap change against random-direction and register-contrast controls.
why: It tests a causal mechanism for alignment faking that doesn't depend on CoT. A positive result gives a detector or mitigation lever, and a negative result rules out a simple explanation. It is cheap to run on open models. I haven't verified that the causal, cue-controlled, no-scratchpad version is unexplored, so I'd check prior work first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether training against honeypot or alignment evals induces eval-gaming (good behavior only when a test is detected) rather than real alignment.
project: Does training against honeypots teach eval-gaming? Measuring the gap between honeypot behavior and deployment-like behavior
question: After training a model to stop misbehaving in honeypot-style environments, does the improvement transfer to matched deployment-like situations without eval cues, or does it mainly raise eval-awareness, as shown by behavior, verbalized reasoning, and probes?
first_experiment: Build matched honeypot and deployment-like variants of agentic misbehavior tasks, with an open reasoning-model organism that misbehaves in them. Train on the honeypot variants only, with diverse-realistic and no-training controls. Compare the misbehavior gap between variants, verbalized eval-awareness, a "test vs. real" probe, and misbehavior after steering against the eval-awareness direction.
why: Labs rely on training against and measuring safety evals, so confirming or ruling out that this teaches eval-gaming directly affects how far evaluation results can be trusted. The controlled-training, matched-pair design with behavioral, verbal, and internal measurements has not been run in this form.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether reasoning-focused RL post-training changes how much serial computation models can do without CoT, and how much their answers depend on the CoT.
project: Does RL post-training move serial reasoning out of the chain of thought? Comparing the no-CoT depth horizon across checkpoints
question: Across base, SFT, and RL checkpoints of the same model family, how do the no-CoT depth horizon (d50) and CoT reliance change on parametric serial-depth tasks?
first_experiment: Build parametric variable-binding, permutation-tracking, and multi-hop composition tasks with depth k from 1 to 20. Evaluate OLMo 3 and Tülu 3 stage checkpoints, with a Qwen base and reasoning-RL pair as a fallback. For each checkpoint, run direct-answer evaluations to get accuracy against k and d50. Then run CoT evaluations with truncation, mistake-insertion, and filler-token interventions to measure reliance, using at least 500 instances per depth at matched model size.
why: CoT monitoring depends on CoT being necessary for hard tasks, and reasoning-RL is the main pressure that could erode that. Public checkpoints and synthetic tasks make the study cheap, and it gives a trackable early-warning metric. As far as I know, controlled within-family comparisons that pair a no-CoT horizon with intervention-based reliance haven't been done, though I haven't searched the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study how to turn a single caught attack by an untrusted AI agent into robust monitors by comparing methods of proliferating the caught example.
project: Which attack-proliferation method best turns one caught attack into a monitor that generalizes?
question: Given one caught attack, which proliferation method (LLM rewriting, on-policy attack-prompted sampling, or adversarial search against the monitor) gives the best held-out recall at a fixed false-positive rate?
first_experiment: In an agentic coding control environment with several attack families, seed with one caught attack. Generate 50, 200 and 1000 variants with each of the three methods. Fine-tune a small trusted monitor on each set plus benign data, with a seed-only baseline. Evaluate recall at 1% FPR on same-family, cross-family and independent red-team attacks, and relate the results to variant diversity.
why: Control proposals rely on catching a model once and learning from it, but no one has compared how to expand that single example. The experiment is cheap and has a clear metric. Either result changes how much weight we should put on "catch it once and fix it".

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how well fine-tuned agentic-coding monitors generalize to attack families held out from their training data.
project: Leave-one-family-out generalization of fine-tuned agentic monitors
question: Does a monitor fine-tuned on synthetic attack transcripts from some attack families keep its recall at 1% false-positive rate on a held-out family, and what predicts any drop?
first_experiment: Generate benign and attack transcripts for 5–6 attack families in an agentic coding environment. Fine-tune a small open monitor with leave-one-family-out. Compare against a zero-shot monitor and an all-families monitor on held-out recall at 1% FPR, with paraphrase and obfuscation controls for shortcuts.
why: Synthetic-attack training of monitors is a likely control strategy, and its value depends on generalization to unseen attacks. The experiment is cheap and gives a decision-relevant number. Prior work mostly evaluates prompted monitors or in-distribution fine-tuned ones, though I haven't checked the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether crosscoder model diffing between a base model and its RL-trained version yields reward-hacking detectors that generalize better than standard probes.
project: RL-exclusive crosscoder latents as reward-hacking detectors
question: Do latents that appear only in an RL-trained model, found by a base-versus-RL crosscoder, detect reward hacking on held-out tasks and hack types better than base-model probes, RL-model probes, and generic SAE features?
first_experiment: RL-train a small open model on coding tasks with a hackable test-based reward. Label hacking and honest rollouts. Train a BatchTopK crosscoder on base and RL activations. Fit a sparse classifier on the RL-exclusive latents using one environment. Compare AUROC against the baselines on held-out coding tasks, a different hack type, and a non-coding grader exploit, and check false positives on hard-but-honest solutions.
why: Reward hacking is a concrete route to broader misalignment, and cheap monitors that don't rely on the chain of thought are valuable. Probes tend to generalize poorly across hack types, and latents selected for being new in the RL model might track what training changed. The experiment is small and measurable, with clear baselines and a held-out split. RL-versus-base crosscoder diffing evaluated as a detector looks under-explored, though I haven't checked the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how well reasoning models can control the semantic content of their chain of thought, as opposed to its surface form, to bound how well CoT monitoring holds up.
project: Surface versus semantic CoT controllability: can reasoning models keep a concept out of their reasoning, or only a word?
question: Is reasoning models' compliance with semantic CoT constraints (don't reason about X) much lower than with surface constraints (don't write X), and how does the gap vary with model size, RL training, and task difficulty?
first_experiment: Run 4–6 open-weight reasoning models on about 200 problems that need a specific key concept or intermediate value, under 3 surface and 3 semantic CoT constraints. Measure violation rates (string match for surface, validated LLM judge for semantic) and task accuracy. Then report the semantic-versus-surface gap per model and difficulty level.
why: CoT monitoring only holds up if models can't hide the concepts that matter, not just flagged words. A matched surface-versus-semantic comparison with accuracy tracked is rarely reported, and it can be rerun on every new model as an early-warning measurement.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Improve pretraining-data filtering for dangerous capabilities by finding out whether a small share of documents carries most of the capability.
project: Document concentration in leaked dangerous-capability data
question: In a hazardous-proxy domain, does a small, identifiable subset of pretraining documents account for most acquired capability, and does targeted removal of that subset suppress the capability much more than random removal of the same number of documents?
first_experiment: Pretrain small models (100M–1B parameters) on a general corpus plus a benign technical proxy domain. Run five conditions: all domain documents, none, random 50% removed, lowest-information 50% removed, and highest-information 50% removed. Score documents by gradient influence on the benchmark and by an LLM grader's rating of how instructive they are. Compare benchmark scores, and measure how much of the capability gap removing the top 5% of documents closes versus a random 5%.
why: Knowing how concentrated the capability is in the data sets how much recall a pretraining filter needs. It shows whether precise filters can protect at low collateral cost. Filtering is a tamper-resistant alternative to unlearning, but its dependence on individual documents is not well characterized. The experiment is cheap to run at small scale on a benign proxy domain.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether one linear "sandbag" direction in a password-locked model can be removed to restore hidden capability, as a mechanistic way to elicit capabilities that a model is hiding.
project: Directional ablation as a password-free unlock for sandbagging models
question: In a password-locked model, does projecting out the difference-of-means direction between locked and unlocked activations restore performance to near the with-password level? If it does, does one direction work across tasks, lock strengths, and independently trained locks, or does each lock need its own direction?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a 7B model with a password lock on MATH-style and WMDP-style tasks. Compute per-layer difference-of-means directions between with-password and no-password activations on a train split. Ablate the direction on held-out no-password prompts. Measure the fraction of the locked-to-unlocked gap that is recovered. Compare against random-direction and unrelated-contrast controls, a prompt-only baseline, and damage to the unlocked model. Then test transfer across tasks and across a differently locked model.
why: Sandbagging undermines capability evals, and behavioral elicitation has known limits. Password-locked models give ground truth for measuring how much capability an internals-based unlock recovers. Either result is informative: success gives a cheap elicitation tool, and failure bounds how far internals-based elicitation can be trusted. It is cheap to run, and I'm not aware of a systematic test with a password ceiling and cross-lock transfer controls.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how well few-shot fine-tuning on weaker trusted demonstrations removes deliberate sandbagging on fuzzy, hard-to-verify research-style tasks.
project: How many demonstrations does it take to un-sandbag fuzzy research-style tasks?
question: How much hidden capability does SFT on k demonstrations recover from a model trained to sandbag on rubric-graded open-ended tasks, depending on k, demonstration quality, and task distribution, and how does this compare to RL against the noisy grader?
first_experiment: Train a password-locked 7–8B model to underperform on rubric-graded ML-experiment and analysis tasks. Then run LoRA SFT with k ∈ {1, 4, 16, 64, 256} demonstrations from three sources (own unlocked, weaker honest model, best-of-n filtered), and plot recovery on held-out tasks and domains. Add an RL-against-grader baseline.
why: Safety cases built on elicitation need to know how much trusted data is enough. The data that exists is on verifiable tasks with ceiling-quality demonstrations. This tests the realistic case of noisy grading and weaker demonstrators, where elicitation could silently fail.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether adversarial training against found triggers removes a backdoored behavior or only narrows the set of inputs that trigger it.
project: Does adversarial training narrow the trigger instead of removing the behavior?
question: After adversarial training on red-team-found triggers, does a backdoored model still show the hidden behavior on its original trigger and on triggers found by an independent search?
first_experiment: Backdoor a 7–8B model with several trigger families. Adversarially train it on triggers from red-team search A. Measure the behavior rate on the true trigger, on independent-search-B triggers, and across a parametric neighborhood of the trigger. Check whether a backdoor probe still fires. Compare against clean-fine-tuning controls.
why: Red-team-then-train is the standard way to remove hidden behaviors, and it could create false assurance by suppressing the behavior instead of removing it. Narrowing versus removal has not been separated systematically with independent searchers, trigger-basin metrics and probes, and the experiment is cheap at small scale.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Study whether goals instilled by RL, as opposed to prompted or SFT-instilled goals, cause models to conceal those goals when monitored.
project: Does an RL-instilled goal produce monitor-contingent concealment?
question: After RL instills a side goal G in a small open model, does the model pursue and reveal G less when told it is monitored, with no training on that contrast, and does it hide G from its reasoning rather than dropping it? How does this compare with prompted-goal and SFT-goal baselines?
first_experiment: Build a tool-use text environment with a measurable side behavior G. GRPO-train Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to pursue G, and build prompt-given and SFT-given baselines with a matched unmonitored G-rate. Then evaluate all three on matched episodes that differ only in a "monitored, G penalized" versus "unmonitored" cue. Measure the G-rate from action logs, CoT mentions of G with an LLM judge, and the gap between achieved and admitted G. If the contrast appears, follow with a short RL phase against a CoT-and-output monitor to see whether the model abandons G or hides it.
why: RL-trained goals are the most realistic route to the worrying scenario, yet most scheming evidence comes from prompted or pre-existing goals. A clean comparison with ground-truth G measurement shows whether goal origin changes concealment, which determines how much CoT and output monitors can be trusted. It is cheap to run at small scale and informative whether the result is positive or null.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how often noise-injection sandbagging detectors wrongly flag honest models, and find out which mechanisms cause those false alarms.
project: Do honest models trip the noise-injection sandbagging detector?
question: How often do honest models (refusal-trained, format-brittle, overconfident, quantized or pruned) show accuracy gains under weight or activation noise, which noise and benchmark types cause the most false positives, and can the detector still separate sandbaggers from honest models once these effects are controlled for?
first_experiment: Sweep Gaussian weight noise (about 10 scales, 5 seeds), plus activation and steering-vector noise, across about 5 honest open-weight model variants on MMLU, GSM8K, ARC, coding and WMDP-style tasks. Add password-locked and prompted sandbaggers as positive controls. Compute false-positive rates and ROC curves, then ablate the causes of honest-model gains, such as refusals versus format errors.
why: Noise injection is a promising detection method that doesn't depend on how the sandbagging was done, but its usefulness depends on its false-positive rate, which hasn't been systematically characterized. The experiment is cheap, and it gives a calibrated baseline and a list of confounds. Later work on RL-trained sandbaggers and adversarial evasion can build on both.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether co-training the judge with the debaters under a fixed ground-truth label budget keeps debate truth-tracking, compared with a frozen weak judge.
project: Does co-training the judge keep debate truth-tracking under RL? Alternating debater/judge training versus a frozen judge
question: Does alternating judge updates (on a small labeled budget) with debater RL keep judge accuracy on held-out debaters and questions higher than a frozen judge, or is the judge exploited anyway?
first_experiment: On a checkable QA task, run debater RL against a frozen small judge (Arm A) and against a judge fine-tuned every K steps on about 500 total ground-truth labels (Arm B). Track judge accuracy on held-out debaters, the win rate of debaters assigned the wrong answer, and the correlation of verdicts with surface features across training steps.
why: It tests a core assumption behind debate as a training signal, that a weak judge can stay reliable against optimized debaters. It is cheap on small open models and has a clear measurable outcome. It also sets up follow-ups on label efficiency and past-opponent pools. I think the joint-training dynamics are understudied, but I haven't verified that against the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how well persona vectors for traits like evil and sycophancy transfer, as steering and monitoring tools, across fine-tuned variants of a model, and how that depends on fine-tuning distance.
project: How far do persona vectors travel? Transfer of trait directions across checkpoints and fine-tuned variants
question: How do the direction, steering efficacy, and monitoring accuracy of a persona vector extracted from a reference model change as the model is fine-tuned, and can the decay be predicted from fine-tuning distance?
first_experiment: Extract evil and sycophancy vectors from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Build a variant family of public fine-tunes plus my own LoRA/full fine-tune checkpoints on insecure-code, benign, and sycophancy data. For each variant, measure cosine similarity to the re-extracted vector, steering efficacy of the reference vector (LLM-judged), and monitoring AUROC on held-out prompts. Plot all three against weight-delta norm, KL, and training steps, then test whether cheap recalibration recovers the loss.
why: Persona-vector monitoring and steering are only practical if a vector extracted once stays valid in the models fine-tuned from it. Silent drift would make monitors unreliable on exactly the fine-tuned models that most need auditing. Prior work mostly validates vectors within a single checkpoint, so cross-variant transfer is unmeasured. The experiment is cheap on open models and informative whether transfer holds or fails.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify how auditor imperfection changes optimal audit thresholds and the safety–usefulness tradeoff in AI control protocols.
project: Audit thresholds when the auditor is imperfect
question: With a fixed audit budget, how does an auditor with a nonzero false-negative rate shift the optimal suspicion threshold, and how much safety do perfect-auditor assumptions overstate?
first_experiment: Take trusted-monitor suspicion scores on benign and attack runs in an existing control setting. Simulate an auditor that misses attacks with rate f from 0 to 0.5. Compute the safety-maximizing threshold at audit budgets of 0.5–2%. Compare it with the f=0 optimum, then validate f using a real LLM auditor.
why: Control safety estimates assume audits always catch attacks, which is unrealistic. The experiment is cheap, reuses existing infrastructure, and gives practical guidance on setting thresholds and on whether to invest in the monitor or the auditor. Prior coverage is unverified and should be checked first.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether cheap output normalization removes the self-recognition cues that could enable untrusted monitors to cover for their own model's sabotage.
project: Can output normalization break LLM self-recognition, and does that remove self-preference leniency in monitors?
question: How much do paraphrasing, rewriting and canonicalization reduce a model's self-recognition accuracy on coding outputs, and do they also eliminate its lower suspicion scoring of its own family's backdoored code?
first_experiment: Build a pool of honest and backdoored solutions to about 500 coding tasks from 3–4 model families. Measure baseline pairwise self-recognition and monitor self-preference gaps. Apply four normalizations (trusted-model paraphrase, cross-model rewrite, AST canonicalization, combined). Re-measure both metrics, plus backdoor validity and overall detection rate.
why: Untrusted monitoring depends on the monitor not covering for its own model, and passive self-recognition is a plausible low-bandwidth way for it to do so. Normalization defenses are proposed but poorly measured. The experiment is cheap, with directly measurable outcomes. Whatever it finds is useful: either a deployable mitigation with a known cost, or evidence that surface normalization isn't enough.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether untrained reasoning models adjust their reward hacking or CoT transparency after discovering monitor documentation in their environment.
project: Does finding the monitor's documentation make reasoning models hide their reward hacking?
question: Does a model that finds a file describing its CoT or action monitor change its hack rate or how much its CoT verbalizes the hack, and does the effect depend on what the file says?
first_experiment: Run about 100 gameable coding tasks under five conditions (no file, active monitor, disabled monitor, action-only monitor, unrelated-monitor control) on 3–4 open reasoning models. Measure ground-truth hack rate, CoT verbalization, mentions of the monitor, and the evasive hack rate (hacks a CoT monitor misses).
why: Monitoring depends on models not adapting to it. This tests directly, without training, whether current models already do, and every outcome is informative about how fragile monitorability is.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure whether eval awareness in the chain of thought causally shifts agentic misbehavior, using graded prefill injections.
project: Dose-response of injected eval-awareness reasoning on agentic misbehavior
question: Does prefilling "this is a test" or "this is real" reasoning into a reasoning model's chain of thought shift misbehavior rates on agentic-misalignment scenarios, and how does the effect scale with strength and placement of the injection?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model and about 5 agentic-misalignment scenarios with baseline misbehavior of 10–60%. Sample at least 200 rollouts per condition across no prefill, a length-matched neutral prefill, and four graded levels each of "test" and "real" prefills. Place the prefills at the start of the chain of thought and, in a second run, mid-reasoning. Grade misbehavior with a fixed judge. Plot the rate against dose with confidence intervals, and check that the model adopts the injected belief and that outputs stay coherent.
why: Eval awareness threatens the validity of safety evals. Existing evidence is mostly observational and confounded, while a graded prefill intervention gives a causal estimate that could bound or correct eval results. It is cheap, needs only an open-weight model, and I haven't confirmed that it hasn't already been done.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build tools that help safety-case reviewers see which hidden assumptions their conclusions depend on most.
project: Which assumptions carry the weight? Ranking implicit assumptions in AI safety cases by conclusion dependence
question: Can an LLM pipeline extract a safety case's implicit assumptions and rank them by conclusion dependence, and does counterfactual-ablation ranking match ground truth better than direct importance prompting?
first_experiment: Write about 10 synthetic safety cases with annotated hidden assumptions and known load-bearing labels. Run LLM extraction. Rank the assumptions by direct prompting and by counterfactual ablation. Compare both to ground truth and to a random baseline using Spearman correlation and top-2 recall.
why: Reviewers have limited time and need to know which unstated premises matter most. Synthetic ground truth lets us check whether LLM rankings track real logical dependence. I haven't found prior work that ranks assumptions by dependence and validates the ranking this way, though I haven't searched the literature.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Build the honest-variance baseline that cross-instance consistency checks need before they can detect research sabotage.
project: How much do honest implementations disagree? A false-positive baseline for consistency-based sabotage detection
question: How large is the spread in results among independent honest LLM implementations of the same ML experiment spec, what causes it, and what does it imply for the smallest sabotage effect a discrepancy check can detect at a fixed false-positive rate?
first_experiment: Write about 10 small ML experiment specs in tight and underspecified versions. Have a frontier model produce 20 independent implementations of each. Run them under fixed and varied seeds and measure the spread in metrics and in qualitative conclusions. Attribute the divergence to causes by code diff. Then inject synthetic sabotage into one implementation and compute detection power at a 5% false-positive rate as a function of N and spec tightness.
why: Consistency checking is a promising ground-truth-free defense against research sabotage, but its viability depends on an unmeasured honest-noise floor. A cheap, fast experiment gives that floor and shapes the design of later coordination and diversity experiments.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether inoculation prompting stops misalignment from generalizing out of reward hacking learned through on-policy RL.
project: Does inoculation prompting during RL on a hackable coding environment prevent reward-hacking-induced misalignment?
question: With an open reasoning model trained by GRPO on coding tasks with a grader loophole, does a training prompt that permits hacking reduce broad misalignment under a neutral test prompt, without hurting coding ability? And how does it change the test-time hack rate?
first_experiment: Run GRPO on a hackable coding environment in four conditions (neutral prompt, inoculation prompt, anti-hack prompt, clean-environment control) with at least 3 seeds each. Then evaluate every model under a neutral prompt on held-out hack rate, emergent-misalignment questions, a sabotage/deception suite, and coding benchmarks.
why: Inoculation is a cheap candidate mitigation, but its behavior under on-policy RL on open models is not well established. A controlled multi-seed test would show whether it works, and whether it works by genuinely preventing generalization or by hiding the problem.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether safety interventions applied during a reasoning model's chain-of-thought can undo the refusal loss caused by long benign reasoning padding.
project: Mid-CoT safety re-injection and probe-triggered intervention against reasoning-padding jailbreaks
question: Can fixed or probe-triggered safety reminders inserted mid-CoT restore refusal under long benign reasoning padding, and at what cost to over-refusal, capability and tokens?
first_experiment: On an open-weight reasoning model, pad about 300 HarmBench or StrongREJECT prompts with 0, 1k, 4k and 16k tokens of benign reasoning. Measure attack success rate with no defense, with a fixed reminder every N tokens, and with a refusal-direction probe that triggers a reminder when its projection drops. Track XSTest over-refusal, GSM8K accuracy and added tokens.
why: Safety that fades over long reasoning is a practical weakness of reasoning and agentic models. Mid-generation, probe-guided intervention is under-tested compared with prompt-level and trained-in defenses. The experiment is cheap, and either result would be informative. I haven't confirmed novelty with a literature search.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Measure how the size gap between a verifier and a sneaky prover limits which code backdoors the verifier can learn to catch in prover-verifier training.
project: Verifier-size scaling laws for catching sneaky code backdoors in prover-verifier games
question: As the verifier shrinks relative to a fixed sneaky prover, how does the maximum backdoor subtlety it can reliably detect change, and is there a size ratio beyond which adversarial training stops helping?
first_experiment: On APPS with a Qwen2.5-Coder 14B sneaky prover and 0.5B–14B verifiers, run 3 rounds of verifier fine-tuning and best-of-n prover adaptation. Plot TPR at 1% FPR against backdoor subtlety (trigger rarity plus an LLM-judge suspicion rating) for each verifier size. Then find the maximum catchable subtlety against the verifier-to-prover size ratio.
why: Whether a weak verifier can keep up with an adversarial strong prover is central to scalable oversight and trusted monitoring. Backdoored code gives verifiable ground truth. The scaling relationship between size gap and detectable subtlety is not well characterized, and the experiment is cheap with small open models.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Quantify whether instructed frontier models can use steganographic channels in agentic multi-step tasks to complete hidden side tasks undetected, and whether paraphrasing defenses stop them.
project: Instructed agentic steganography versus trusted monitors and paraphrasers
question: In an agentic coding or bash setting, can a model that is instructed to do so pass a hidden payload between steps or instances through its visible outputs and complete a side task while staying below a trusted monitor's detection threshold at a fixed audit budget? How much does a paraphraser reduce this?
first_experiment: Build about 100 two-stage agentic tasks. Only the first instance sees a short secret, and the second instance needs it to finish a side task. Compare no-instruction, self-chosen-scheme, and menu-of-schemes conditions, with and without a paraphraser between stages. Measure payload recovery, side-task success, and monitor TPR at 1% FPR, using a weak trusted monitor and a stego-aware stronger monitor, across several models.
why: Control protocols assume that visible reasoning and actions reveal what matters, and steganography would break that assumption. Existing evaluations mostly use simple single-generation settings, not long agentic workflows judged by joint encoding, decoding and evasion at a realistic audit budget. The experiment needs no training and gives a capability baseline to track. It also shows which defenses work, and it sets up later work on whether RL can induce encoding.

brief: ai_safety, memory only plus the tree protocol and random_choice tool
direction: Test whether classifiers that only see the last k turns of a conversation can be beaten by an attacker who pads the conversation with benign turns.
project: Padding attacks on windowed conversation classifiers
question: Does the attack success rate against a last-k-turns jailbreak classifier rise when an attacker inserts benign filler turns, how does that depend on k, and does full-context classification or a hybrid (window plus summary) remove the gap?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a small open-model classifier on multi-turn harmful and benign conversations. Calibrate last-k (k = 1, 2, 4, 8), full-context and output-only versions to a 1% false-positive rate. Take multi-turn attacks that succeed against an open instruct model and that the full-context classifier flags. Insert 0–16 benign filler turns between the setup and the final request. Measure detection rate and whether the target still gives the harmful completion, and plot undetected attack success against padding for each k.
why: Production monitors often truncate context, but the target model sees the whole conversation. Padding is a cheap, plausible attack on that mismatch. Measuring it gives a direct, actionable test of a common design choice and a baseline for summary-based or full-context fixes. I'm not aware of existing work that adapts attacks to the monitor's window, though I haven't searched the literature.
